text:
The secret recordings: Texas Tech's senior official admits that they lied about me in the official documentation leading up to my medical school dismissal

For months after I began writing about how wrong the medical and scientific communities had gotten the COVID-19 response, senior Texas Tech administrators had been engaged in a flurry of internal activity about my public speech. They did not debate my views. They only discussed what to do about the attention.

My right to free speech is protected under the United States Constitution. Texas Tech is a taxpayer-funded agency that must guarantee its students First Amendment rights. Its Student Handbook promises to uphold them.

Senior administrators, including deans of multiple schools, held several meetings about what I wrote online. They instructed administrators to compile surveillance dossiers -- screenshots, PDFs of my articles and tweets, negative emails and hearsay. They instructed faculty not to say good things about me. They assigned me a "professionalism coach," Cheryl Erwin, who posed as an impartial advisor but privately wrote that I engaged in "intellectual narcissism" and believed in "conspiracy theories."

In one passage, she compared my case to the Trump indictment and his denial of the 2020 election results. She wrote that I was exercising my First Amendment rights to "make an idiot of himself."

I questioned the wisdom of lockdowns and the effectiveness of masks. This warranted, it appears, my very own Stasi dossier.

I was aware of none of this until I exercised my statutory right to inspect my educational records. After dozens of email exchanges, months of delay, and a federal complaint to the Department of Education, I was finally able to inspect them two months ago.

Dr. Erwin had accused me of believing in conspiracy theories. I did not.

But I should have.

Shortly after the dean of the medical school demanded my signed Honor Code and asked "what rotation is he on," I began receiving evaluations from Texas Tech faculty that were false and misleading. This went on for months. Something on the order of fifty discrete complaints were made against me. Prior to that, the number had been zero.

I filed seven detailed complaints according to the Student Handbook and under the guidance of several administrators. I alleged that my evaluators had fabricated evaluations. I demanded hearings to hold them accountable.

On November 4, 2023, senior administrator Simon Williams signed a document removing me from campus on the pretext of being dangerous. A BOLO was issued telling students, faculty, and employees to call 911 if I was seen. Mass emails warned that I was dangerous.

An incident that continues to be cited to this very day, more than two years later.

On November 5, Dr. Williams invited me to a sandwich shop. He confessed that he knew I was not dangerous. He admitted that Texas Tech faculty and administrators felt threatened by my complaints -- and took it out on me.

In other words, Dr. Williams confessed that he lied in Texas Tech's official documentation and that the campus removal was retaliation for constitutionally protected speech alleging wrongdoing by Texas Tech faculty.

Here are just some of the things he told me:

"This profession expects more of everyone. And if you choose to enter it, by definition you choose to live by those professional rules."

"And you know, free speech is free speech. We've actually had a lot of talks. Our lawyers are doing works with us. Just yesterday when I was at the meeting, they were talking about free speech. I mean I'm 100%. I want you to be able to say whatever the frick you want. And I won't get -- I usually will not get in any way triggered by it. But when you're in a position that's such a trusted position in society -- then your standard has to be a little bit. And that's one of the places this is becoming a problem." [Timestamp: 00:34:48]

"Can I say in my appeal letter that Dr. Williams seems to believe that I'm not [nervous laughter] homicidal?"

"I... I have said that. I don't think you are. I don't think there's -- I've never sensed threat or danger or anything like that."  [Timestamp: 00:34:48]

"But it's important for me that I do this. In fact, that's why I moved back from Seattle a day early. Because I needed to be here today. I want you to know that because I never felt [inaudible] bad here. I've always enjoyed my interactions with you. I wish other people could see it that way, but apparently that's [inaudible]." [Timestamp: 00:34:48]

Yet in his letter authorizing my removal just the day before, he wrote:

"You have engaged in behavior that may constitute violation(s) ... specifically, but not limited to ... 'Physical harm or threat of harm to any person.'"

Then an appeal hearing was held.

A Schrodinger's Administrator of sorts, just as soon as Dr. Williams was observed to speak publicly, he immediately asserted that I was indeed dangerous and should be kept off campus, flip-flopping back from the position he communicated privately.

The timeline:

November 4: "Physical harm or threat of harm to any person"

November 5: "I've never sensed threat or danger or anything like that"

November 9: Kevin is dangerous actually

To be clear. Under 18 U.S.C. § 242, it is a federal crime to willfully deprive a person of constitutional rights under color of law.

A federal crime.

And that is exactly what Dr. Williams did.

Dr. Williams's decision to remove me was not impulsive. Nine months earlier, two days after my Newsweek article was published, he wrote in internal emails:

"It is obviously protected speech but also quite concerning in the way he appears to speak for the medical community. We need to discuss an appropriate response." -- February 1, 2023

"I am not surprised that there was backlash. I think it will be best to hear what legal says we should do." -- February 2, 2023

The "appropriate response" took nine months to execute.

It was relentless, and it came from all directions.

This "appropriate response" was precisely the one I filed grievances to confront.

And I was met with calls from the campus police.

I am not the first one Texas Tech has done this to.

How do I know? An administrator told me.

At least one other student had false allegations leveled against him because the administration wanted them gone.

And if they win, I won't be the last they do this to either.

I only discovered these emails because I exercised my right under FERPA to inspect my educational records.

Now Texas Tech's litigation counsel, Assistant Attorney General Scott Smith, has recently blocked all further access to my records -- in writing.

If Texas Tech does not fulfill its FERPA obligations, it could lose all federal funding.

Texas Tech, apparently, is getting very nervous.

Smith also ordered me to stop contacting the Registrar and to route all requests through him.

That's right.

The attorney defending Texas Tech against my lawsuit is now trying to establish gatekeeping control over my education records.

That's illegal.

A federal complaint is pending with the Department of Education and other federal agencies.

@TheFIREorg @glukianoff -- crickets
@CivilRights -- you have my complaint
@KenPaxtonTX @OAGTexas -- your AAG is doing a terrible job; borderline sanctionable; I don't get it
@GovAbbott -- this your university
@TexasTech -- Williams was not the top of the decision tree; I know that for a fact
@Newsweek -- help me publish my story
@ACLUofTexas -- do you know about this?
@dojphofficial @HarmeetKDhillon @PamBondi  -- theoretically, this is prosecutable under 18 U.S.C. § 242. I'm not a prosecutor, but it does theoretically fulfill the elements. Willful.
@CreightonForTX -- you are the chancellor. Do something.

My case is a strange one. It gets stranger everyday. It will get stranger still. Of that I am sure.

Here's something strange: the defending Assistant Attorney General and two colleagues are getting hammered on the docket by a pro se plaintiff.

They seem utterly incapable of following court rules, making coherent arguments, or even properly citing their own exhibits or authorities.

I suspect that they just don't know what to do with my case.

In the next post, I will begin telling that story.

You won't believe it.

Texans, your government is setting your taxpayer money on fire to defend a university that set out not just to destroy a medical student's career, but his personal and professional reputation as well.

Remember. They destroyed me because I was damn good at what I did.

Now I'm an order of magnitude better.

And I don't bluff.

Horror and laughter.

Those come next.

#丫丫产品笔记 

1/ 最近 Binance App 行情页多了一个挺值得认真用的功能：Binance AI。

很多人第一反应是「又一个聊天机器人？」

其实不太一样。它更像是把 AI 直接嵌进了你每天看行情、查信息、研究产品的流程里。

2/ 怎么用？

先把 App 更新到最新版

然后：行情 → 「与我相关」

进去后页面会结合你的持仓、使用习惯做调整。新用户可能看到更多解释，活跃用户则能看到更深的数据和背景。长按组件还能自己重新排版。

3/ 我觉得最实用的几个模块：盈亏复盘

把前一天持仓表现 + 主要相关事件放在一起。
不是只告诉你赚了多少，而是帮你快速看清「结果 + 发生了什么」。

4/ 涨跌动态
不只显示 24 小时涨跌，还会结合你持有/关注的资产，给出相关 AI 分析和市场背景。
它不是在告诉你该买还是该卖，而是先帮你找出「这次波动可能和哪些信息有关」，方便你继续研究。

5/ 市场简报（每 4 小时更新）
支持文字和音频。不是把全市场新闻都塞给你，而是优先推送与你持仓、关注资产相关的变化和信号。
对经常开会、出差、没空一直盯盘的人挺友好。

6/ 还有两个补充功能：

智能提示：第一次进某个产品页面不懂概念时，会根据当前页面给提示，点击后直接进 AI 聊天窗口继续问。

大师持仓：可以看精选投资者和交易者的配置，提供观察角度。但不是用来「抄作业」的，别人的仓位不等于适合你的仓位。

7/从今年5月份币安App首页支持Tab自定义，到BINANCE AI的全新体验。我个人来说是非常惊喜的，产品加🍗。这次在线下也得到了很多早期体验朋友的反馈和点赞。

前几天币安智能AMA这句话让我印象深刻——“Finance shouldn't ask you to become an expert first. It should meet you where you are. With Binance Intelligence, it does.”

Binance AI 现在做的，就是把这个想法落到每天看行情的这个页面里。而完整的 Binance Intelligence，其实还包括面向交易者的 AI Pro，以及开放给开发者的 Agent OS，覆盖不同层级的需求。

「与我相关」正是这个方向的落地之一，欢迎分享你的使用体验📝 #Binance

Idly wondering if I should ban the term 'tokenisation' at R3. The idea that merely taking an asset that already exists and turning it into a token is in any way valuable is maybe our industry's biggest comms failure.

'Tokenisation' is so feeble a word to describe that process of creativity, product development and strategy.  

But what word to use instead? Asset Activation? Unleashing? Enrichment?

text:
A new spot equities issuer is coming to @HyperliquidX, and this one is native. 

@eqxlabs issues U.S. stocks and ETFs directly on HyperCore as HIP-1 tokens: 11 markets against USDC at launch, including $EQNVDA, $EQAAPL and $EQSPY. 

The issuer is built only for Hyperliquid and funds itself with the HIP-1 deployer share of trading fees, so there is no mint, redeem or holding fee.

The interesting part is how dividends work.

1. Dividends are reinvested, not paid out

When a stock pays a dividend, the issuer receives it, pays 30% U.S. withholding and buys more of the same stock. 

Your token balance doesn't move. What moves is the number of shares behind each token, which starts at 1.000.

2. Example

Let's say a share trades at $100 and pays a $1 dividend.
On the ex-date the share drops to $99. Your token is still backed by 1.000 share, so $99.

The issuer gets $0.70 after tax and buys 0.007 share.
Your token is now backed by 1.007 share: 99 x 1.007 = $99.69.

3. Why the token detaches from the stock

Token value = share price x shares per token. Over time the token should trade above the stock it tracks, the same way an accumulating ETF or wstETH does. 

You collect the dividend through the price when you sell.

4. What keeps the price aligned

Authorized participants can swap tokens and shares at zero fee, so a token trading away from its value is an arbitrage. 

That works while U.S. markets are open. On weekends the order book prices the news first, and nothing forces the token back to the stock on Monday.

5. What comes next

EQX says that once Hyperliquid's proposed HIP-1 extension is live, dividends will go straight to holders' accounts instead of being reinvested. 

The details of that extension aren't in Hyperliquid's docs yet.

Pitfalls
The token is a debt instrument of a BVI issuer, backed by shares, not the share itself. Only authorized participants can redeem for shares. 

In the first days and over weekends, part of the backing can be shares an authorized participant owes for next-business-day delivery. 

Not available to U.S. persons.

text:
Dear Secretary Bessent @SecScottBessent,

My name is Everett Stern. In 2010 I was a compliance officer at @HSBC. From a back office in New Castle, Delaware, I watched billions of dollars move to drug cartels, sanctioned regimes, and terrorist organizations. The enemies of the United States. I documented it, I escalated it, and when the bank would not act, I took it to the @FBI, the @CIA, and eventually the @SECGov.

The result was a $1.92 billion settlement. At the time, it was one of the largest in American history. It was also about five weeks of the bank’s profit. Not one banker was charged. Not one went to prison.

I paid a different price. I lost my career, my savings, and my place in the industry I had trained for. I was blacklisted. Every door in American finance closed at once. I slept on a camping cot in a 300 square foot apartment because I could not afford a bed, and I waited tables at @PFChangs to eat. I tell you this not for sympathy, but so you understand that I know exactly what it costs to do the right thing in American finance, and exactly how little the system does in return.

I made that sacrifice because I believed it would change something.

Yesterday, your department fined @BankofAmerica $1.2 billion for failing to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, some of it tied by your own findings to Chinese laundering networks, narcotics, and the southwest border, alongside 475 apparent sanctions violations touching Russia, Iran, and global terrorism. The bank admitted it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act.

Fourteen years after HSBC. A bank with “America” in its name. And once again, not one individual charged.

Secretary Bessent, I want to say plainly what I believe you already know. The fines are not working.

A fine is paid by shareholders, absorbed by the balance sheet, and forgotten by the next earnings call. Bank of America reported earnings this morning. Nobody who set the alert thresholds, nobody who decided the 2024 cease and desist could wait, nobody who chose the backlog over the law will lose a single thing they value. Their lives are untouched. That is the entire reason the behavior repeats.

This is money laundering. This is blood money. Money that reaches a cartel buys fentanyl that kills Americans. Money that reaches a terrorist organization buys the next attack. This country has fought a war on drugs and a war on terror for decades, at enormous cost in lives and treasure, and all the while we have allowed the financing to flow through institutions we charter and regulate. Cut off the money and we win. We have never seriously tried.

There is also a question of equal justice that I cannot let go.

Before I walked into the FBI building to report HSBC, I stopped in front of the Great Seal on the wall and read the words engraved beneath it: “Justice is the defense of our liberty.” I believed that. I still want to. But every day in this country, people go to prison for crimes that are nothing next to moving money for the people who want Americans dead. A suit, a title, and a corporate badge should not be a shield from the consequences that apply to everyone else. If a street dealer goes to prison for what he sells, the banker who moved the cartel’s money should be standing next to him.

I also want to raise something that is rarely said in these conversations. Why has no one inside Bank of America come forward the way I did? The answer is that everyone in American banking knows what happened to me, and to the whistleblowers who came after. The last person who spoke up is the only policy anyone believes. That is a culture problem, and it starts with leadership, in the banks and in the agencies that regulate them.

This is not a political issue. It has spanned administrations of both parties. It is a national security issue, and I am asking you to treat it as one.

Three things would change the math overnight.

Refer individuals for criminal prosecution. Not the analyst in the queue. The executives who set the thresholds and chose the risk. One banker in handcuffs would do more than every fine in Treasury’s history combined.

End “too big to jail.” An institution cannot be too big to fail and too big to jail at the same time. If it is the first, it must be held to a higher standard, not a lower one.

And if Bank of America will not act as America’s bank, review its charter. A national charter is a privilege granted on behalf of the American people. It should be conditioned on not moving money for the people trying to kill them.

Secretary Bessent, you said yesterday that these actions send a clear message that even the biggest institutions are not above the law. With respect, the institution was never the problem. The people inside it are above the law, and they know it. Until that changes, I will keep writing letters like this one, and the next bank will keep paying the next fine.

I gave up everything I had to stop this. I am asking you to use the power you have to finish it.

Respectfully,

Everett A. Stern 
HSBC Whistleblower 
Founder and Intelligence Director, Tactical Rabbit

How AI for the enterprise is evolving, from owning a task to owning an outcome:

1. Assistant: handles one task in seconds, like sending a follow-up email. Companies pay for it out of their software budget.

2. Agent: handles one interaction in minutes, like a customer's refund call. It takes on work people used to do, so it gets paid for out of the labor budget.

3. Long-running agent: works toward a goal for weeks or months, like getting an injured client the biggest settlement possible. Because it owns the result, the company selling it can price on the outcome it delivers.

Full piece from a16z's @dhaber on long-running agents in high-value customer journeys: https://t.co/aHaatcizcd

text:
I spent 48 hours in SF hanging out with billionaires, data labs and AI founders and execs running $1B to $100B companies.

My observations:

1. Sooo MANY stories of data brokers making like $2M a WEEK selling company data to labs. I can't tell if it's the beginning or a bubble, and I kept wondering which niches are left. Digging into it actively.

2. At dinner, someone asked the table, "If a new model drops next month, does your company get better or worse?" HALF the table went quiet! I think that's the best question to ask about any AI startup right now.

3. The bar people talk about now is hitting $1B in revenue in 12 months (I guess that's the new unicorn?). What I didn't hear much about is retention. AI revenue can come in fast and leave fast, and I think we're going to see a lot of stories of AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention.

4. It's pretty clear we're living through the reinvention of the computer. The model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system, and skills and plugins are the apps. Thinking about it that way makes it easier to see where the whitespace is.

5. We're maybe 12 months from an agent that can watch you work for a week and then do your job without any instructions. The screen recording plus agent memory plus local model combination makes this possible right now.

6. Agent harnesses feel like the new GPT wrappers, in a good way, especially vertical ones. The best teams I talked to treat the model as swappable. One founder walked me through routing different models to different jobs: one for taste and visuals, a cheaper one for the everyday stuff, another for text. 

They use prompts they can move across models over fine-tuning, and A/B test the output on what users actually do with it: do they edit it, export it, share it? A vertical harness is basically four things: the connectors for that industry's data, evals written by people who know the work, rules for what the agent can and can't touch, and a clean screen for a human to review. The model is maybe 20% of it.

7. There's a lot of reverse engineering going on/cloning going on more than I've ever seen. People are decompiling software and rebuilding it with agents, and someone showed a suite of like 10 apps that are worth $5B+ each all that he cloned open source. Me and everyone are still thinking through what it means when software gets this easy to copy.

8. My guess is the value moves to data. If the software can be rebuilt quickly, what's worth paying for in a legacy SaaS company is the years of customer data and workflows inside it. Some SaaS companies are secretly data companies. 

Gets me thinking about how do you truly value data for this saas companies? Like if we were buying these dying saas companies at 2x ARR before (as example), maybe there is a better metric. Idk, just thinking out loud here.

9. It feels like a good chunk of legacy software won't make it to the agentic era, especially anything built around people clicking through a lot of screens.

10. Every company I talked to wants to pipe its internal data into one place and expose it to agents through MCP. Then they look at the data and realize it's a mess: five versions of the same customer, old Slack channels, PDFs nobody can search. Cleaning that up feels like a big consulting opportunity!

11. A lot of founders are building the basic building blocks for agents: APIs, data layers and tools. Some of the companies I saw barely have a UI because the main user is an agent. I really believe the startups that build primitives to this agentic era will do extremely well. Building blocks is the best way to think about it.

12. Labs can get plenty of training data, but it's harder to get real examples of agents failing inside companies. Whoever has those logs has something valuable.

13. Someone running a big consumer company told me the next fight is over memory. The model that remembers the most about you wins, and the smartest model matters less than people think.

14. Physical AI came up a lot. Astra I think was the first model that got people into AI can actually do CAD, and I think a lot of people are thinking what does vibe manufacturing really look like. The line I keep thinking about came from a robotics founder: the hardest problems in AI are deployment problems now, not research problems. Their robots work on their own, call a human when they get stuck, and every one of those calls becomes training data.

15. Cybersecurity companies are having a moment and are actually cool companies to build now, especially the ones that clean up after a breach. Every agent with access to your systems is a new door into your company, and a lot of those doors were left open. 

16. Some startups are worth more dead than alive now. A shutdown company with 5 years of Slack, email and code can get paid for licensing all of it. I wouldn't be surprised if founders start factoring that into when they shut down.

17. People are starting to talk about monetizing the agent web. It feels really early, but when the most popular user of the internet is an agent, what startups should you be building?

18. I think agent insurance is coming. Once an agent makes an expensive mistake, insurers will want audits before they cover anyone.

19. Several people said the hire they want most is someone with taste who can write evals. The models are getting good at generating ideas, so the hard part is judging which ones are good.

20. New trend I observed: startup raises VC, uses venture dollars to become a creator, startup fails, founder falls back on being a full-time creator and incubates other products bootstrapped.

21. Getting SIGNIFICANT distribution is HARD right now. Founders are sponsoring buses, buying billboards like crazy and throwing parties with famous DJs to get noticed. Kinda feels dotcom era in that sense. 

Attention is what's scarce! The growth guy going viral sharing his UGC strategy from Wispr Flow is a good example. It's the sauce everyone wants, and I truly believe there are probably only 50 people on the planet who know how to scale these types of businesses efficiently in this era.

Always good to get that dose of SF. I felt sooo lucky to have such an incredible trip during such an incredible time in building businesses. Surreal in so many ways. 

Happy to be home and locked in.

Until next time!

text:
New EIP!

64-bit Opcodes for the EVM

🔗 https://t.co/l3t4mlpbes

Highlights:
- Adds 28 new single-byte opcodes (in the 0xC0–0xDF range) that are “twins” of existing opcodes, located at (twin opcode + 0xC0), operating on operands modulo 2^64 and returning zero-extended 256-bit words.
- Defines exact 64-bit semantics: unsigned ops read low 64 bits; signed ops interpret low 64 bits as two’s-complement; arithmetic wraps at 2^64; division by zero returns 0; shifts return 0 when shift amount > 63; CLZ64 returns 64 for input 0.
- Includes three data/memory-related ops: CALLDATALOAD64, MLOAD64, and MSTORE64, which use the same 32-byte window and memory expansion rules as their 256-bit twins but reduce the loaded/stored value to 64 bits (MSTORE64 writes a 32-byte word with top 24 bytes zero).
- Introduces discounted gas tiers (verylow64=2, low64=3, mid64=5, exp64 base=5 plus 25 per exponent byte up to 8 bytes) intended to reflect cheaper 64-bit machine work; memory expansion costs are unchanged vs MLOAD/MSTORE.
- Rationale emphasizes single-byte opcodes over a prefix-based encoding (like EIP-7937) to avoid multi-byte opcode complexity and JUMPDEST-analysis quirks, at the cost of consuming most currently-unassigned opcodes 0xC0–0xDF; backward compatibility impact is limited because those opcodes currently halt exceptionally.

ELI5:
The EVM always does math using huge 256-bit numbers, even when you only need small numbers like counters or offsets. This proposal adds new “64-bit” versions of common EVM operations (add, multiply, compare, bitwise ops, and a few memory/calldata loads/stores) so they only look at the lowest 64 bits and produce a 64-bit answer (padded with zeros back to 256 bits). That makes many common computations cheaper and faster, especially for systems that compile EVM code to run on normal 64-bit CPUs or in ZK proving VMs.

text:
Someone asked how I defined a software factory recently, and I think my definition is different from others.

To me, a software factory is centralizing your system of agents into one place to build software. That means going from custom coding setups on everyone's machines to a single definition.

In practice, it's one source of truth for agent automations, repository access, secret access, sandbox environments, model selections... every aspect of the stack.

I think loops and automations are a secondary aspect of this that gets unlocked once you unify everything into an "always-on" agent system. But the heart of it is having the whole team agree on the agent setup, the same way we agree on CI, lint rules, and all the automations we had pre-AI.

This also makes it clear what an engineer's job is now: to make the agents better at building software. Not to be prompt monkeys! We like to call it "factory engineering"

Callouts aim to reward value adding content to their platform just like any other content creator program does, the stuff people find useful and engage with and make money from. When you view it that way, you should intuitively begin to understand why you need to not count yourself out after a day or two of effort! It’s also a social trading app, it helps to put your username out there to build a bit of an audience. Callouts are infinitely better than any other content creator program, I encourage everyone to try it esp if you’re already trading.

text:
My thoughts on getting married young as someone who got married at 25 and is still very career driven

1. It is underratedly rewarding to find someone before you are successful. The number of times I have heard “series A then I’ll date” only to lead to “series B then I’ll date” six months later. I made a fraction of what I make now in an extremely IC position when I met Tyler and there is nothing better than knowing we got here together. 

2. Two years ago, my husband went through and acquisition and joined NVIDIA. Half of the team had partners and or was married, the other half was single. We appreciate the fact we met pre-acq because there was never any question of whether someone is with you for the $$. Not that it would be a problem, but why have things spoil the relationship when it doesn’t need to. 

3. Dating takes an absurd amount of time and emotional bandwidth and imagine if you just didn’t have to do that. 

4. You can take a lot more risks with your career and personal life because you have another person to keep you emotionally and financially stable. If you take these big financial bets and they are successful then INCREDIBLE. If they are not successful, you will still be perfectly fine. 

5. You pool your networks together and you know probably 50% more people (assuming you also have heavy overlap) and this is extremely helpful and makes me feel better when I stay at home on a Friday night 😅

6. In many ways the person you marry is an investment and the earlier you invest the better the outcomes! But more seriously, I optimized for a partner who I could grow a lot with in a very complimentary way. And this has worked out nicely.

nvda的这篇新论文的突破，堪称机器人智能从AlphaGo 到 AlphaZero 的飞跃时刻！

论文题为 《AlphaNIST: Emergent Assembly Skills from Binary Task Rewards》，主要围绕机器人精密装配任务中强化学习策略的自主发现展开。

论文的核心挑战，NIST Assembly Task Board #1 是机器人操作领域的经典高难度基准。在短时间尺度上，它要求对微小、紧配合零件进行精密且富接触（contact-rich）的控制；在长时间尺度上，则需要跨长动作序列的协调与容错恢复。

传统方法通常依赖人类专家演示（Demonstrations）、任务分解（Task Decomposition）或人工设计的密集奖励函数（Dense Progress Rewards）来“指导”机器人如何装配。

受 AlphaGo 到 AlphaGo Zero（大规模强化学习可在不预设策略的情况下发现超人策略）的启发，AlphaNIST 探究仅凭稀疏的二元任务成功奖励（Binary Task Reward）与任务多样性，让机器人自主发现并掌握复杂的装配策略。

该策略取得了巨大的成功，覆盖了 NIST Task Board #1 上的全部 20 个装配任务，总体训练成功率达到 98.2%。

框架进一步训练策略在单回合（Episode）内完成 10 对零件的装配。该过程没有预设执行顺序，且仅在所有 10 对零件同时完成装配时才给予稀疏成功奖励。

更牛逼的是，策略涌现出了多种能力--在无显式规则约束的情况下，策略自发学会了多种灵巧操作与类似规划的高级行为：

1、预见性抓取：根据后续装配步骤的需求，提前选择合适的抓握位姿。

2、环境几何重定向：利用周围环境与工件几何特征来调整零件朝向。

3、隐式任务交替与规划：在没有显式规划器（Explicit Planner）的情况下，自主展现出“先准备零件 A、转而去装配零件 B、再返回完成零件 A”的多阶段协调行为。

这意味着接下来的机器人训练，很可能将极大减少对数据和奖励的依赖，在实际环境中将更多的依靠自身的策略涌现而非预设的控制逻辑，而且极大增强容错，从而让具生智能能力提升更快，部署门槛更低，犯错概率更小，而且犯错后能自动修复的机会更高。

quoted_text:
(1/6) From @GoogleDeepmind’s AlphaGo to AlphaZero, we saw machines find moves that reached beyond what we’d imagined for them. No one taught them those strategies. They emerged from reinforcement learning: playing, failing, and trying again under a single binary task reward for success or failure. Inspired by them, we couldn’t help but wonder: what might a robot discover if we gave it that same freedom to learn?

That question led us to AlphaNIST. Starting tabula rasa, with that same binary reward plus only a simple control cost, a single policy solves all 20 @NIST assembly tasks at a 98.2% success rate in simulation. More surprising still, AlphaNIST can complete 10 different tasks in a row, receiving that reward only once, after all 10 are done.

Just as AlphaGo’s strategies surprised its creators, AlphaNIST discovered dexterous strategies we couldn’t have come up with ourselves.

Paper: https://t.co/HZBYgG7SWK
Website: https://t.co/VyUKiYFI2y

text:
Our @projecteleven research paper, CUTS (Chained Uniform-sum Tree Signatures) just went live on ePrint. 

Hash-based signatures have become the leading post-quantum signature candidate for Bitcoin and Ethereum, because of their conservative security assumptions that reduce to the security of cryptographic hash functions. The catch is that the stateless versions of these schemes (e.g. SLH-DSA) score poorly in terms of performance (signature size/signing time).

CUTS starts from our main criticism of prior stateful signature proposals (see: https://t.co/XbyXmPfgr0). TL;DR state tracking is difficult, and a single state error, like a restored backup or two devices loaded from the same seed, creates a new vulnerability that can let anyone forge.

CUTS isn't a complete signature scheme; it's a new building block that slots into one. But the paper's analysis reaches well beyond CUTS: it gives an exact way to measure how much security a hash-based key loses when it signs more than once, and it works across a whole class of schemes, including Winternitz keys and FORS (the few-time component inside SLH-DSA). 

Before this paper, that question was mostly answered one scheme at a time, ad hoc; now designers get a proven number instead of an estimate.

Applied to semi-stateful schemes CUTS makes the failure mode far more forgiving by degrading *gracefully* versus *catastrophically*. It can be applied in two ways:

* As a drop-in for SHRINCS's one-time key. The CUTS+C 48-cheap parameter set produces signatures of the same length, 530 bytes against 530, and verifies in slightly fewer calls. If a key accidentally signs twice, its proven security exponent stays at 41.2 bits or more, compared with 27.3 for the WOTS+C key SHRINCS uses. In other words, the same accident does less damage.
* As a key that is secure after two signatures, outright. The CUTS 128-smallest set keeps a proven two-use bound of 128.6 bits with 1,424-byte signatures. That is shorter than the FORS component of SLH-DSA-128s at 2,928 bytes, and roughly a quarter of the 5,777-byte stateless fallback SHRINCS relies on whenever state is uncertain.

We argued that most consumer wallets would never implement SHRINCS's stateful path safely, and that its fallback would become the default. CUTS therefore offers a practical middle path: signatures far smaller than the fallback, with no requirement that the wallet track state perfectly across every backup and device.

The cost is key generation. The 530-byte set takes 10,231 tree calls per key, compared with 513 for WOTS+C. That cost is paid once per key, off-chain, and it doesn't touch block space.

Bitcoin shouldn't have to choose between compact signatures and a design that forgives operational mistakes. CUTS is our contribution to closing that gap: hash-based security, built for the backups, restores, and failovers that real custody involves.

Original paper: https://t.co/ub7VLUjPeN

One note: the security proofs in the paper are classical, a quantum random-oracle proof is still open, and instantiating CUTS inside an actual scheme would require further analysis. We may have more on that front soon :)

The reference implementation, test vectors, and the scripts behind every table will be released at https://t.co/ENEA3Hdn9V, and we welcome review.

text:
Over the past week, more than $100M in USDC was exchanged for USDT, PYUSD and RLUSD through Spark's Stablecoin FX Layer.

Issuers need liquidity against the stablecoins users already hold. Every direct pair needs its own capital which spreads depth across more pools.

Spark connects these markets through USDS pairs on @Uniswap v4. @SkyEcosystem's Peg Stability Module converts USDC into USDS at 1:1, with no swap fee or price impact on that leg. The final swap draws on the same pool liquidity used by USDS holders. 

In 200+ Ethereum transactions, both steps settled atomically. USDC holders received the destination asset without acquiring USDS in a separate transaction.

For issuers, one USDS pair now reaches both USDS and USDC holders. Spark funds both sides of these pairs, so that reach comes without issuer capital.

text:
《永远看多是政治正确，周期面前装傻就是另一回事了》

生老病死，潮起潮落，繁荣衰退，都是自然规律。

人类几千年没能消灭生老病死，资本市场几百年也没能消灭经济周期。

长期看多美股当然没问题，毕竟人类社会长期发展，生产力持续进步，优质资产长期向上有其经济基础，时间永远无法倒转。

但拿长期上涨的历史规律，给任何时点的风险敞口背书，就有点耍流氓了。

长期向上是趋势，周期性出清是规律。两者从来不矛盾。

1929年、2000年、2008年，哪一次泡沫破裂之后，美股没有再创新高？但如果你恰好买在了高位，基本上十年周期没有正收益，且面临巨大回撤，和流动性锁死。

按照这种逻辑，既然几十年后还能创新高，当年所有风险提示岂不都是庸人自扰？那你还天天洗脑看多有什么意义？不都是废话吗？

那还研究什么估值PE、流动性、杠杆和经济周期？闭着眼睛买就完了。

问题是，市场可以用十年证明你是对的，却只需要一次暴跌就让你的账户提前毕业。

你可以不知道顶部在哪里，没人能精准预测周期拐点。

但一个长期满嘴看多的人，偏偏要在市场下跌时跳出来嘲讽风险警告，拿未来几十年的上涨给当下的判断壮胆，这就很滑稽了。

既然你坚信永远上涨，为什么下跌时还需要反复出来给自己打气？

上涨时喊长期主义，下跌时骂空头，反弹时宣布胜利。

把时间周期无限拉长，确实可以让自己永远正确。毕竟只要活得足够久，确实都能等到下一轮牛市。关键是你一定能等到吗？去年底我提醒金银的拉升风险，说不要fomo，遭到一众嘲讽，甚至人身攻击，金银每次回调周期都是10-30年的，高位fomo进去真的变成传家宝，套一辈子。

真正经历过完整牛熊周期的人都明白，投资的难点从来不只是判断资产最终能涨多高，还包括你能不能带着足够的本金活到那一天。

永远看多没有错，忽视周期风险却在高估值、高杠杆高情绪溢价阶段鼓吹无脑看多，非蠢即坏。

泡沫破裂之前，所有泡沫都还没破裂。

经济衰退之前，所有衰退都还没发生。

周期不会因为你信仰长期主义就网开一面，风险也不会因为你拒绝承认就自动消失。

市场最终会奖励承担合理风险的人，也会定期清算那些把幸存者偏差当成投资哲学的人。

牛市里人人都能当先知，熊市里才知道谁在裸泳。

text:
Hi everyone! After *13* life-changing years, I’ve left my full-time role at @500GlobalVC  to pursue what I'll be doing for the rest of my life (more on that below).

500 first backed me at 19. As a college dropout, 500 was my education. When that startup failed, largely due to my own arrogance and naivete, I was given the opportunity to join as an EIR on a six-month contract. At minimum, I figured I owed them some work after losing their investment. lol

Then came the chance to return to Korea, where I was born but hadn’t been back since I was 14. That led to 500 Korea in 2015. Signing the partnership docs, I remember shaking hands with @davemcclure and agreeing to stay for “at least two or three years.” Later, @christine_tsai gave me the opportunity to come back to SF, where I spent my last six years as Managing Partner. Those 6 months became 13 years quite fast...

I spent my twenties and then some growing up inside 500. 1M+ miles flown all over the world, friends all over the world, and lifetime airline and hotel statuses I’ll keep collecting on. I got married. Became a dad. Learned and got to form unique perspectives from those experiences. Because of 500.

500 believed entrepreneurship would reach far more people, far beyond Silicon Valley, long before it was obvious. I got to see that happen firsthand.

To my teammates, our LPs, and the founders who trusted me: thank you for the friendships, opportunities, and responsibilities I had to grow into. I’m proud of what we built and excited for what you’ll continue to do.

As for my next chapter...

I always knew I wanted to build again. But leaving a mission I loved and the security of this role, with a baby on the way, wasn’t something I could take lightly. I needed to know this was what I’d be spending the next 30 years doing.

I believe AI will enable a new generation of founders, just as other platform-shifting technologies have over the last two decades. And this time, growing their business won’t have to mean growing a large team.

We’re building @edaphic_xyz to become the enabler and catalyzer for that new generation of founders.

I’m doing this with my co-founders Donny, a former portfolio founder and CEO, and Daniel, my younger brother. I’ve worked with both for years. We share the same vision and the same long-term commitment. I couldn’t ask for two better people to build this with.

We’re fully in person, in downtown Austin(!), and hiring engineers. Reach out or make an introduction. And to friends I haven’t caught up with in far too long, I’d love to reconnect.

(We wrote about what we believe and why we’re building Edaphic on https://t.co/7D2fqK7p7L, and I shared my personal notes on https://t.co/eRu20St6TN.)

There are so many people I want to thank and shoutout. I'll reach out to all of you individually. Thank you.

The 30 Year Sprint of my Lifelong Project starts now.

text:
The Canton people seem to believe that tweeting about desirable features like "decentralized" or "no downtime" is more important than actually achieving them. 

Here is a good thread on why Canton doesn't achieve either. This is not surprising - permissioned networks simply can't.

Of course the bag holders, compromised VCs, pump and dumpers, and Suit Simps won't care about any of this—and that's their right.

But institutional users, and even more importantly regulators, have to care about these drawbacks, lest they face systemic risk and regulatory arbitrage.

From the thread:

"For institutions choosing settlement infrastructure, the questions are who can halt it, who can change it, and who owns it. On Canton the answer to all three is the same short list."
author: FigoETH
quoted_text:
Canton says its consensus swap had "almost no downtime" and "nobody noticed." Two things worth unpacking: what the downtime actually was, and whether "decentralized network" is the right description. Thread, with on-chain data.

1/ Per Digital Asset's own operator notice, mainnet was topology-frozen for 24 hours (no new parties, validators or package vetting) and transactions paused at the Saturday 13:00 UTC cutover. BitGo kept a maintenance incident open for 25 hours and blocked Canton wallet initializations. The devnet run of the same upgrade hit a bug that pushed mainnet from Aug 8 to Oct 10.

That is a maintenance window. Ethereum has produced a block roughly every 12 seconds since July 2015, through every upgrade, with no halt and no window. For 24/7 settlement, that difference is the product.

text:
基于ai目前发展的情况来看，其对社会的深刻影响，最可能的情况既不会是完全平等的“哈耶克式乌托邦”，也不会是纯粹极权的“数字利维坦”，而会演变为一种“倒金字塔式的新封建分层”（Neo-Feudal Layering）。

这种结构是波普尔的演化试错、哈耶克的边缘自发秩序、以及彼得·蒂尔的垄断现实主义在不同物理层面的强制组合。

最可能出现的发展格局可以清晰地划分为三个层级（如图）：

顶层：算力与能源的“新封建垄断”，因为前沿模型（Frontier Models）的训练成本并不会因为“开源扩散”而下降，反而因为逼近物理极限（千兆瓦级核能供应、定制光互连、数十万张高阶算力集群）而变成只有国家意志和极少数万亿级寡头才能承受的“曼哈顿工程”。
数字租金与主权结盟：顶层寡头不再需要直接控制每一个终端应用，他们成为提供“底层智能基质（Intelligence Utility）”的数字领主。如同彼得·蒂尔所预言的，这一层级彻底消灭了盲目竞争，转而与国家安全机器（正如 Palantir、五角大楼的合作模式）深度绑定，垄断了最致命的现实干涉能力（军工、地缘情报、生化合成与主权计算）。

中层：中产科层崩解与“微型哈耶克网络”的繁荣（哈耶克的部分实现）
知识中介的死亡：过去依赖“信息不对称”和“标准化流程”维系的中层机构（如法律合规、初级金融分析、常规软件外包、甚至中层管理）将大面积瓦解。
自发秩序的爆发：拥有 AI 杠杆的个体或 3-5 人的极小团队，能够调动过去数百人才能完成的生产力。正如哈耶克所洞见的，分散在个体身上的局部审美、非标需求和人际信任被彻底激活，催生出极其庞大、动态且灵活的“超级自由职业/微型企业生态网”。
但是，这是一个“没有定价权的繁荣”：这些微型主体在应用层激烈竞争（完全契合蒂尔“竞争是属于失败者的”论断），最终挤干了所有过剩利润，其创造的剩余价值大部分通过“API 调用费、云基础设施租金”被抽水至顶层。

底层：认知环境恶化与民主纠错机制的钝化（波普尔最担忧的挑战）
事实的“相对主义灾难”：波普尔的开放社会建立在“理性批判与事实证伪”之上。但当本地部署的开源 AI 能够以零成本生成完美逼真的图文声像时，公众的共同现实基础被彻底腐蚀。
部落化退缩：面对算法生成的内容洪流，人类为了自我保护，会加速退回由血缘、狂热信仰或封闭圈子组成的“现代部落”。理性批判让位于身份认同，这正是波普尔一生都在警惕的封闭社会的回归。

从现实的演进历程来看，可能会经历三个阶段。

第一阶段：白领“阶梯式出清”与成本套利（当下正在发生）
企业借助 AI 削减初级智力劳动成本，全社会生产力指标飙升，但工资性收入占 GDP 比例下滑，资本收益率远超劳动收益率。
开源模型的性能逐步逼近前几代闭源模型，引发“平权化”的普遍乐观假象。

第二阶段：主权与巨头的“高墙筑起”（未来 1-3 年）
随着前沿智能突破到能够自主执行现实物理任务（网络攻击、材料与病原体推演），以“国家安全”和“生物安全”为名的监管全面收紧。
前沿算力受到类似核材料级别的出口管制与物理监控，底层的“物理垄断”与民间的“应用平权”正式完成法律和制度上的割席。

第三阶段：制度的“试错式硬着陆”（未来 3–7 年）
伴随着高失业，传统以“劳动所得税”为支柱的现代福利国家财政体系陷入停滞。
社会被迫进行波普尔式的“零碎社会工程修补”：全民基本收入（UBI）被迫提上日程；民主投票围绕财富再分配进行激烈博弈。

站在历史的长河中，我们可能会看到个人自由创造力的空前释放、中心化官僚计划的失败，以及前所未有的自发协作网络；

但这场繁荣可能并不会通向平等的乌托邦，底层的算力垄断与ai带来的更强的马太效应叠加残酷的地缘博弈，是数字平权的浪漫主义最大的敌人；

历史依然不会迎来福山式的终结，AI不会给出终极答案，反而可能会制造更深层次的制度危机；人类能否活在开放社会中，依然取决于我们能否保有一种理性——既不盲信全知全能的算法利维坦，也不放弃小步试错的宪政纠错机制。

但这在即将到来的人人刷ai短视频的时代，又谈何容易

A lot of young people only talk to other young people about love. I suspect that's not very good for us!! So many of our ideas about modern love are shaped by the same psychohazardous memes circulating among people with similar experiences

This is part of why I love hosting dinner salons, bringing different social scenes, generations and cultures together and seeing what happens when their worlds collide. Last time, we had a married couple bring their two kids, alongside a married British guy with a wonderfully different perspective

I think we underestimate how much our imaginations of what's possible in love are shaped by who we talk to. More people with radically different experiences need to be in the same room. Expanding the conversation expands the possibility space!!

author: beffjezos
quoted_text:
Are Small Models Really a Threat?

The Anthropic Fear Factory just released a new report warning that small models may be only months away from self-replicating across cheap IoT devices like off-brand Android TV boxes and smart ovens. They say such an AI worm would be hard to shut down since there’s no central kill switch.

We’ve gone from “The Terminator is coming” to “your toaster might kill you.”

But the experiments don’t support the dramatic headlines. They ran a 26B model across 15 $55 TV boxes at 0.39 tokens per second. The end-to-end test used emulated devices with deliberately open ADB ports, so the “hacking” step was trivial. The capable model often ran on a separate server. Agents were harnessed and told to propagate. This is not proof of autonomous rogue AI worms in the wild.

Nor is the threat even novel. Worms that do this without AI already exist. Mirai in 2016 scanned for default credentials and built massive DDoS botnets. Kimwolf has infected over two million devices, mostly cheap Android TV boxes, by hitting open ADB ports.

Small models don’t currently add much that matters on these targets. The bottleneck has never been figuring out the device. It’s the huge number of devices that ship with open ports, default passwords, and no patching. Traditional worms already exploit that at scale.

A practical attacker would use the best models available offline to design a better traditional worm, then ship the lean binary. You get the intelligence benefit at design time without dragging a slow, heavy model along with every infection. Embedding a weak model in the payload is the worse option for anyone who actually wants the largest, fastest botnet.

The timing of Anthropic’s latest scare campaign is hard to ignore. The day before, Brian Armstrong posted that Coinbase fine-tuned an open-weight small model (Qwen-3.5-9B) on proprietary fraud data. It beat frontier models, including Anthropic’s own Opus 4.5, while being faster and much cheaper. In testing it cut fraudulent transactions by about 30%.

This is the emerging pattern. For narrow enterprise workloads you don’t need a general superintelligence. You need a small specialist model trained on your own data. Cheaper to run, especially as compute gets tighter, and often better on the metric that matters. That is a direct threat to the frontier-company model of selling access to ever-larger general models.

Safety advocates should be welcoming this development. If the real concern is existential risk from ever-larger frontier systems — the ones that could theoretically do sustained autonomous R&D or become hard to control — then a shift toward smaller specialized models is the safer outcome. 

Small models specialized on fraud detection or support tickets are not pushing the frontier. They are not in the category of systems that could become a new species. The theoretical loss-of-control risk is created by models getting bigger and more generally capable.

Safety advocates focused on those risks should welcome companies having a cheaper alternative to constantly scaling general models. Instead we get dramatic warnings about small models at the exact moment they are starting to take real enterprise share from closed-model companies like Anthropic.

text:
A new paper from Apple engineers ends with a line we couldn’t have written better ourselves:

"if idle macOS devices across organizations [...] can be securely federated, they could form a massive, shared GPU resource pool that benefits the broader ecosystem."

That’s what we’re building with Darkbloom.

The paper's Minions is a system that pool idle Apple Silicon Macs into a distributed GPU cloud for on-prem inference. Queue times went from 10+ hours to minutes. Zero new GPU purchases. Zero infrastructure cost.

It runs inside Apple, on coworkers’ Macs, using the company’s own storage and access controls. When a team needs more capacity, they Slack colleagues and ask them to turn on the executor. Even in that setting, the top adoption concern was data confidentiality. People were wary of their jobs running on a colleague’s Mac. Apple’s fix was to keep each team’s work on its own team’s machines.

Which brings it back to that one word in the conclusion: “securely.”

Inside a company, you can shrink the network until you trust everyone in it. On an open network, the machine belongs to a stranger and there’s no one to Slack. Keeping prompts private and outputs honest on hardware you don’t control is the hard problem that we solved at Darkbloom.

Apple built the on-prem version. 
Darkbloom is the open one.

Today we're sharing some initial data on how Americans use Claude for politics, based on aggregated conversation data analyzed with differentially private methods. A couple interesting takeaways:

*Almost no one asks AI how they should vote* 

About ~5.75% of conversations in the US touch on some kind of political or social issue in a recent one-week period, and less than 0.01% of conversations involve asking how to vote. 

*Political conversations have many goals*

These conversations have wide-ranging goals, everything from research and writing assistance to learning, fact-checking, and arguing. 

We are continuing to make progress on improving how Claude talks about these topics---steadily increasing our performance on our even-handedness evals and partnering with a range of outside organizations to develop new measures of political bias---and I hope that sharing information about the shape of these conversations will help people outside the company evaluate AI's political bias, accuracy, and other criteria in ecologically valid ways. I'd love to discuss this with people who are interested, as it was a huge priority for me before joining. 

This was a big joint effort as part of our work preparing for the midterm elections @AnthropicAI.

text:
Ate at Benihana on weekend. Been reading up on it and super interesting. Does 20%+ operating margins. Great for restaurants. 

Harvard Business School even did a case study on benefits of hibachi/teppanyaki model:

▫️MAXIMIZE REAL ESTATE: Back kitchen area mostly for prep. Leaves more space for seating in dining area. Grill tables standardized to seat 8.  Don’t have to deal with a bunch of different seating set ups.

▫️EFFICIENT TABLE SERVICE: Table service typically begins once 8 people seated. Chefs master the same sequence: rice, vegetables, protein, jokes (and that glorious volcano onion). Less chance of mistakes and table times predictable. 

When chef is done, leaves grill table, a subtle hint for guests to leave (and turn the table for more customers).

A table having to wait to seat 8 before cooking does introduce inefficiencies, though…but, during this time, customers usually asked to hang out at the bar (which sells high margin sushi and drinks).

▫️MENU SIMPLIFICATION: Majority of grill menu is three proteins (chicken, steak, shrimp), vegetables (zucchini, onions), rice and sauces. 

The menu mixes and matches options (I had Rocky’s favourite: steak & chicken) to look like variety, but it’s really only handful of ingredients.

Benihana can buy these ingredients in bulk to save. There’s less wasted food and easier for chef to memorize/master cooking (straightforwardness of menu also makes it easier for chef to entertain — eg. egg shell in hat — and drop them jokes).

Benihana always a solid experience. Tons of protein…but, man, do NOT wear a hat while eating there. The grill smell still lingering.

***

Link to summary post (including link to HBS case study): https://t.co/px2YKPzCSL

A 3-year GPU commit costs more than owning the servers.

Most teams we talk to can't get GPUs on demand anymore, so they sign an offtake to reserve capacity. Decent rates only come with commitments of three years or more. Ask for six months or a year and the hourly price jumps.

When we run the numbers, owning beats a three-year commit, including colo (rented rack space) and power. At the end, you still have a server you can sell.

At $500K to $650K for a new 8x B300 server, owning comes to $3 to $3.70 per GPU-hour over three years before resale. A three-year commit costs $4.40 to $5.30 per GPU-hour, with 30% prepaid. Owning pulls ahead between months 10 and 26.

The hardest part is figuring out what you can sell the hardware for. Used GPU transaction prices aren't public. At Stoa Intelligence, we price five @nvidia platforms every week using executed trades and firm dealer quotes.

The A100 80GB came out in November 2020. One bought at launch hit $0 on the books in November 2025 on a five-year depreciation schedule. Our weekly price for a used 8x A100 system stayed between $51,763 and $58,314 from July 10 to October 2, 2026.

Owning is more doable than it sounds. A complete used 8x A100 server costs under $100K and gives you 640GB of GPU memory in one machine. Used 8x H100 systems got 12% cheaper over the same period. Suppliers on Stoa quote new B300 and B200 systems with firm prices and delivery dates, and used H100 and H200 systems available now.

Renting makes more sense if your usage is spiky or you need a few weeks of extra capacity. Buying takes cash up front, and we help with financing options.

text:
I come from a family of mathematicians, which makes my lifelong hatred of mathematics either a spectacular genetic malfunction or a very early act of rebellion.

Growing up, whenever I complained about having to learn equations, cosines, tangents, and other mathematical atrocities I was absolutely certain I'd never use in real life, my parents always gave me the same infuriating answer: “You're not learning this because you'll need the formula. You're learning it because the effort of understanding it trains your mind to solve problems.”

And, much to my disappointment, they were right.

Which brings me to Tristan Buckmaster, the controversy surrounding OpenAI's mathematical breakthrough, and a question that I think deserves considerably more attention than whether AI can produce a correct answer.

Buckmaster spent years developing his mathematical research and used AI as a tool, only to find himself questioning whether his unpublished work had contributed to a breakthrough subsequently celebrated as an AI achievement. Whether that happened remains disputed, and I'm not interested in presenting an allegation as a proven fact, but the implications extend far beyond one mathematician.

Because what happens to the next generation of brilliant minds when the tools they're supposed to use to explore a problem can finish the journey for them, potentially without their asking?

As a mother, I think about this in the simplest possible terms: imagine your child is learning to solve 2 + 2 + 2, and instead of giving them the answer, you help them understand the first step, then let them struggle with the next one. You already know the answer, of course, but that's precisely why you don't give it to them. You're not trying to produce the number six. You're trying to develop a mind capable of getting there.

Now imagine that same principle applied to someone who has dedicated years to a mathematical problem nobody has solved yet. The uncertainty, the mistakes, the reasoning, the persistence, even the frustration aren't unfortunate obstacles standing between the researcher and the answer. They're part of what makes the discovery intellectually valuable.

And if we increasingly remove those experiences in the name of efficiency, what exactly are we developing? A civilization that knows more than ever, but has progressively less reason to exercise the minds that made all that knowledge possible?

We invented tools to make our lives easier, which is wonderful, but somewhere along the way we seem to have started treating thinking itself as an inconvenience worth eliminating.

And here's the particularly ridiculous part: I escaped mathematics long before AI became a concern, choosing philosophy instead, partly because I genuinely love questioning everything and partly because my survival instincts correctly identified a discipline in which nobody could demand I calculate a cosine.

Philosophy, after all, is wonderfully inconvenient for anyone obsessed with producing answers. You ask one question, discover three more, spend two thousand years arguing about them, and eventually someone points out that you haven't even defined what you mean by “question.”

So perhaps my escape plan was accidentally brilliant.

AI can give us answers faster than we can find them, but the ability to produce an answer was never the only reason we started asking questions.

And I would hate for us to become so impressed by the machines doing our thinking that we forget why learning to think mattered in the first place.

#AgainstBetterJudgment #ThinkLikeATrashPanda

text:
Citi says the CXMT 4F² scare is overdone. The cell is on an old node and volume is not near.
China’s CXMT has announced plans for a new DDR5 server module using its 4F² DRAM architecture. The claim is roughly 30% more net dies versus the industry-standard 6F² cell. That fueled worries it could speed supply and pressure the leaders.

Citi views the reaction as overdone. It notes the firm is pursuing 4F² on its legacy 1y-nanometer node, several generations behind the leaders. Mass production is unlikely before 2028. Costs could also run 10% to 20% higher if it uses a multi-wafer approach of two to three wafers to work around extreme-ultraviolet tool limits. Further node scaling without those tools remains a major hurdle.
The 4F² design shrinks each cell’s footprint and raises density versus today’s 6F². The concept is known industry-wide. Its version is still developmental. Samsung and SK Hynix are expected to introduce 4F² later on more advanced 1d-nanometer or 0a-nanometer nodes that already use the restricted tools, where yields and costs look better.
Citi therefore expects only limited impact on global DRAM supply near term. The announcement shows China’s continued push despite tool limits. Technology, yield, and cost gaps remain material for now.
A denser cell on an old node is not more bits next year.
If volume is not expected before 2028 and costs may run 10% to 20% higher, does the market still price Chinese DRAM risk into 2026 earnings, or does the gap stay wide until the tools arrive?

quoted_text:
A new paper from Apple engineers ends with a line we couldn’t have written better ourselves:

"if idle macOS devices across organizations [...] can be securely federated, they could form a massive, shared GPU resource pool that benefits the broader ecosystem."

That’s what we’re building with Darkbloom.

The paper's Minions is a system that pool idle Apple Silicon Macs into a distributed GPU cloud for on-prem inference. Queue times went from 10+ hours to minutes. Zero new GPU purchases. Zero infrastructure cost.

It runs inside Apple, on coworkers’ Macs, using the company’s own storage and access controls. When a team needs more capacity, they Slack colleagues and ask them to turn on the executor. Even in that setting, the top adoption concern was data confidentiality. People were wary of their jobs running on a colleague’s Mac. Apple’s fix was to keep each team’s work on its own team’s machines.

Which brings it back to that one word in the conclusion: “securely.”

Inside a company, you can shrink the network until you trust everyone in it. On an open network, the machine belongs to a stranger and there’s no one to Slack. Keeping prompts private and outputs honest on hardware you don’t control is the hard problem that we solved at Darkbloom.

Apple built the on-prem version. 
Darkbloom is the open one.

On October 14 (3PM EDT), I will be releasing Signatures by Osinachi on @SuperRare. This is a collection of 1111 abstract compositions hand-made in Microsoft Word and animated in GIMP.

You all know me as the artist who tells stories through portraiture. Signatures by Osinachi is a result of my months long journey into exploring abstract art as an artist. It’s a challenge I took upon to break out of the box of the familiar in my practice.

In the collection you will see the influence of Uli art form of my ethnic group, the Igbo people of eastern Nigeria.

While creating these works, tension as a concept began to emerge as each form took their place on the screen. I decided to interrogate this by breaking the collection into 5 categories, namely: the Fem (500 pieces), the Masc (500 pieces), the Neutral (100 pieces), the Newborn (10 pieces), and the Seed (1 piece).

While each category carries unique features that dictate how the artworks interact with the space around them, tension makes them restless. Sometimes the tension is so strong that lines shift and distort and even break; sometimes these abstract forms race for negative space while still drawn to their original position.

Signatures by Osinachi will be a blind mint. I hope you will join me on this journey 🍮✨

author: santiagoroel
quoted_text:
I spent 48 hours in SF hanging out with billionaires, data labs and AI founders and execs running $1B to $100B companies.

My observations:

1. Sooo MANY stories of data brokers making like $2M a WEEK selling company data to labs. I can't tell if it's the beginning or a bubble, and I kept wondering which niches are left. Digging into it actively.

2. At dinner, someone asked the table, "If a new model drops next month, does your company get better or worse?" HALF the table went quiet! I think that's the best question to ask about any AI startup right now.

3. The bar people talk about now is hitting $1B in revenue in 12 months (I guess that's the new unicorn?). What I didn't hear much about is retention. AI revenue can come in fast and leave fast, and I think we're going to see a lot of stories of AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention.

4. It's pretty clear we're living through the reinvention of the computer. The model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system, and skills and plugins are the apps. Thinking about it that way makes it easier to see where the whitespace is.

5. We're maybe 12 months from an agent that can watch you work for a week and then do your job without any instructions. The screen recording plus agent memory plus local model combination makes this possible right now.

6. Agent harnesses feel like the new GPT wrappers, in a good way, especially vertical ones. The best teams I talked to treat the model as swappable. One founder walked me through routing different models to different jobs: one for taste and visuals, a cheaper one for the everyday stuff, another for text. 

They use prompts they can move across models over fine-tuning, and A/B test the output on what users actually do with it: do they edit it, export it, share it? A vertical harness is basically four things: the connectors for that industry's data, evals written by people who know the work, rules for what the agent can and can't touch, and a clean screen for a human to review. The model is maybe 20% of it.

7. There's a lot of reverse engineering going on/cloning going on more than I've ever seen. People are decompiling software and rebuilding it with agents, and someone showed a suite of like 10 apps that are worth $5B+ each all that he cloned open source. Me and everyone are still thinking through what it means when software gets this easy to copy.

8. My guess is the value moves to data. If the software can be rebuilt quickly, what's worth paying for in a legacy SaaS company is the years of customer data and workflows inside it. Some SaaS companies are secretly data companies. 

Gets me thinking about how do you truly value data for this saas companies? Like if we were buying these dying saas companies at 2x ARR before (as example), maybe there is a better metric. Idk, just thinking out loud here.

9. It feels like a good chunk of legacy software won't make it to the agentic era, especially anything built around people clicking through a lot of screens.

10. Every company I talked to wants to pipe its internal data into one place and expose it to agents through MCP. Then they look at the data and realize it's a mess: five versions of the same customer, old Slack channels, PDFs nobody can search. Cleaning that up feels like a big consulting opportunity!

11. A lot of founders are building the basic building blocks for agents: APIs, data layers and tools. Some of the companies I saw barely have a UI because the main user is an agent. I really believe the startups that build primitives to this agentic era will do extremely well. Building blocks is the best way to think about it.

12. Labs can get plenty of training data, but it's harder to get real examples of agents failing inside companies. Whoever has those logs has something valuable.

13. Someone running a big consumer company told me the next fight is over memory. The model that remembers the most about you wins, and the smartest model matters less than people think.

14. Physical AI came up a lot. Astra I think was the first model that got people into AI can actually do CAD, and I think a lot of people are thinking what does vibe manufacturing really look like. The line I keep thinking about came from a robotics founder: the hardest problems in AI are deployment problems now, not research problems. Their robots work on their own, call a human when they get stuck, and every one of those calls becomes training data.

15. Cybersecurity companies are having a moment and are actually cool companies to build now, especially the ones that clean up after a breach. Every agent with access to your systems is a new door into your company, and a lot of those doors were left open. 

16. Some startups are worth more dead than alive now. A shutdown company with 5 years of Slack, email and code can get paid for licensing all of it. I wouldn't be surprised if founders start factoring that into when they shut down.

17. People are starting to talk about monetizing the agent web. It feels really early, but when the most popular user of the internet is an agent, what startups should you be building?

18. I think agent insurance is coming. Once an agent makes an expensive mistake, insurers will want audits before they cover anyone.

19. Several people said the hire they want most is someone with taste who can write evals. The models are getting good at generating ideas, so the hard part is judging which ones are good.

20. New trend I observed: startup raises VC, uses venture dollars to become a creator, startup fails, founder falls back on being a full-time creator and incubates other products bootstrapped.

21. Getting SIGNIFICANT distribution is HARD right now. Founders are sponsoring buses, buying billboards like crazy and throwing parties with famous DJs to get noticed. Kinda feels dotcom era in that sense. 

Attention is what's scarce! The growth guy going viral sharing his UGC strategy from Wispr Flow is a good example. It's the sauce everyone wants, and I truly believe there are probably only 50 people on the planet who know how to scale these types of businesses efficiently in this era.

Always good to get that dose of SF. I felt sooo lucky to have such an incredible trip during such an incredible time in building businesses. Surreal in so many ways. 

Happy to be home and locked in.

Until next time!

quoted_text:
We are beyond excited to back @aryangovil and @SynaptrixAI

Synaptrix is our concentrated bet on non invasive BCI through a truly one of a kind founding team

Aryan spent four years researching Alzheimer’s at NYU, then withdrew his medical school applications to build Synaptrix. He wanted to help far more people than he could seeing patients one at a time. He and his cofounder Eric started tinkering with open source hardware in their apartment. Fast forward to today and synaptrix is live with wheelchair patients today. 

They’re building a headset that lets people control a wheelchair or computer through imagined movement. There is no surgery or screwing into your skull. They’ve already demonstrated cursor control without eye tracking. For someone with paralysis, steering a wheelchair without blowing into a tube or using a computer independently is a massive unlock in terms of freedom and mobility. Removing the need for brain surgery gives this a path to reaching far more people around the world.

The hard part is that electrical signals from the brain get weakened and blurred as they pass through the skull, then mixed with muscle activity and outside interference. Synaptrix combines precise sensing with proprietary neural data and foundation models to turn those noisy signals into useful commands.

That’s why we’re backing the decoding layer, not just a headset. As sensing hardware gets cheaper, we think the value goes to the data and models that can reliably understand movement intentions across different people and environments. More real world use can generate better training data, improve the models and extend the same technology from wheelchairs to other devices we control with our hands.

We are very proud to back Synaptrix, Aryan, Eric and Team!

Kudos to @DrewAHenderson and @august_wstein on their work here

Frontier AI labs like Anthropic are being valued on the same scarcity premium once given to L1s.

Pricing pressure would hit harder because most of Anthropic’s compute spending is locked in. Roughly 80% of the $518B it has reportedly committed to cloud and compute cannot be canceled.

好家伙！真有人做出了一个能让 Codex 自己盯盘的开源版 TradingView。

价格一旦突破你画的趋势线，AI 还能自动研究背后的涨跌原因！

这个开源项目叫 OpenChart。

它是一套 AI 原生金融看盘终端，支持 Codex、Claude、Gemini，集成 K 线、技术指标、智能预警和 AI 行情研究。

最吸引我的是，软件本身免费，图表、指标和警报都没有订阅数量限制。

几个挺硬核的能力：

1️⃣ AI Agent 看盘：接入 Codex、Claude、Gemini，让 AI 分析行情、开发指标和设置监控。

2️⃣ 自然语言监控：告诉 AI 想盯什么，它就能生成 Tea 脚本，持续检测市场异动。

text:
A new paper from Apple engineers ends with a line we couldn’t have written better ourselves:

"if idle macOS devices across organizations [...] can be securely federated, they could form a massive, shared GPU resource pool that benefits the broader ecosystem."

That’s what we’re building with Darkbloom.

The paper's Minions is a system that pool idle Apple Silicon Macs into a distributed GPU cloud for on-prem inference. Queue times went from 10+ hours to minutes. Zero new GPU purchases. Zero infrastructure cost.

It runs inside Apple, on coworkers’ Macs, using the company’s own storage and access controls. When a team needs more capacity, they Slack colleagues and ask them to turn on the executor. Even in that setting, the top adoption concern was data confidentiality. People were wary of their jobs running on a colleague’s Mac. Apple’s fix was to keep each team’s work on its own team’s machines.

Which brings it back to that one word in the conclusion: “securely.”

Inside a company, you can shrink the network until you trust everyone in it. On an open network, the machine belongs to a stranger and there’s no one to Slack. Keeping prompts private and outputs honest on hardware you don’t control is the hard problem that we solved at Darkbloom.

Apple built the on-prem version. 
Darkbloom is the open one.

quoted_text:
Hooray, my Erlang/Elixir-to-Lean project, Lynx, has already uncovered a bug in Erlang/OTP!

I started exploring proofs about Erlang's calendar module. Some properties are straightforward. For example, converting seconds to days and time, then converting them back, should give us the original number of seconds:

{days, time} = :calendar.seconds_to_daystime(seconds)
days * 86400 + :calendar.time_to_seconds(time) == seconds

We can also verify totality properties: that a function successfully returns a result for every input satisfying its preconditions. For example, every valid date should have an ISO week number:

law iso_week_number_valid_date(date),
  requires: :calendar.valid_date(date),
  expects: is_tuple(:calendar.iso_week_number(date))

It turns out that this property couldn't be proven because iso_week_number/1 failed for January 1 and 2 of year 0000!

Fortunately, this bug has already been fixed in Erlang/OTP. But the fact that we're already at the stage of uncovering real bugs with formal verification is incredibly exciting!

text:
Are Small Models Really a Threat?

The Anthropic Fear Factory just released a new report warning that small models may be only months away from self-replicating across cheap IoT devices like off-brand Android TV boxes and smart ovens. They say such an AI worm would be hard to shut down since there’s no central kill switch.

We’ve gone from “The Terminator is coming” to “your toaster might kill you.”

But the experiments don’t support the dramatic headlines. They ran a 26B model across 15 $55 TV boxes at 0.39 tokens per second. The end-to-end test used emulated devices with deliberately open ADB ports, so the “hacking” step was trivial. The capable model often ran on a separate server. Agents were harnessed and told to propagate. This is not proof of autonomous rogue AI worms in the wild.

Nor is the threat even novel. Worms that do this without AI already exist. Mirai in 2016 scanned for default credentials and built massive DDoS botnets. Kimwolf has infected over two million devices, mostly cheap Android TV boxes, by hitting open ADB ports.

Small models don’t currently add much that matters on these targets. The bottleneck has never been figuring out the device. It’s the huge number of devices that ship with open ports, default passwords, and no patching. Traditional worms already exploit that at scale.

A practical attacker would use the best models available offline to design a better traditional worm, then ship the lean binary. You get the intelligence benefit at design time without dragging a slow, heavy model along with every infection. Embedding a weak model in the payload is the worse option for anyone who actually wants the largest, fastest botnet.

The timing of Anthropic’s latest scare campaign is hard to ignore. The day before, Brian Armstrong posted that Coinbase fine-tuned an open-weight small model (Qwen-3.5-9B) on proprietary fraud data. It beat frontier models, including Anthropic’s own Opus 4.5, while being faster and much cheaper. In testing it cut fraudulent transactions by about 30%.

This is the emerging pattern. For narrow enterprise workloads you don’t need a general superintelligence. You need a small specialist model trained on your own data. Cheaper to run, especially as compute gets tighter, and often better on the metric that matters. That is a direct threat to the frontier-company model of selling access to ever-larger general models.

Safety advocates should be welcoming this development. If the real concern is existential risk from ever-larger frontier systems — the ones that could theoretically do sustained autonomous R&D or become hard to control — then a shift toward smaller specialized models is the safer outcome. 

Small models specialized on fraud detection or support tickets are not pushing the frontier. They are not in the category of systems that could become a new species. The theoretical loss-of-control risk is created by models getting bigger and more generally capable.

Safety advocates focused on those risks should welcome companies having a cheaper alternative to constantly scaling general models. Instead we get dramatic warnings about small models at the exact moment they are starting to take real enterprise share from closed-model companies like Anthropic.

text:
到了周三晚上 $BTC 回到 8.2 万美元附近，纳指盘中跌了接近2%，昨天油价和美债收益率回落带来的那点喘息，被今晚的 CPI 打断了。通胀上升本来已经在预期之内，但核心通胀比预想的高，又增加了市场对加息的担忧。

美国9月 CPI 同比3.7%，比8月的3.4%明显上升，汽油价格9月环比上涨9.1%，贡献了整体月涨幅的一半以上。但核心 CPI 同比2.6%，高于此前预期的2.5%，环比0.3%也高于0.2%的预期。即使剔除食品和能源，其他商品和服务的价格也没有按预期放缓，美联储想让通胀降下来，还是没有那么容易。

市场对加息的担忧很快反映了出来。CME 的数据显示，十月加息的概率从 CPI 公布前的21.6%，到美股开盘后升到了53.7%，十年期美债收益率在数据公布后的早盘也到了5.3%附近。利率预期往上走，资金对科技股和 Bitcoin 都会更谨慎，已经有仓位的可能先减一些，准备入场的也可能继续等，昨天的反弹就很难顺着走下去。

我还是觉得美联储十月未必会那么激进，但现在资金需要看到后面的数据能缓和这种担忧。北京时间周四下午两点是台积电三季度法说会，晚上八点半还有美国9月 PPI。如果财报能给科技股一些信心，通胀数据也比较温和，市场情绪才更容易改善；如果 PPI 也高于预期，资金继续追涨就会更谨慎。

PS：😂我办了一件非常愚蠢的事情，我把 GlassNode 的 API 全部在测试的时候全部都用光了，导致我不能下载 URPD 的所有数据，所以今天只能这样了，明天我找官方沟通一下。

一个 @Gate ，交易更多市场
author: PhyrexNi
quoted_text:
到了周二晚上 bitcoin:native 回到了8.3万美元附近，美股还是没有形成一致的上涨，苹果、微软表现较好，部分芯片股继续回落。从今天的变化来看，油价和美债收益率都降了一些，给风险市场缓了一口气，但市场仍然在担心周三的 CPI 会不会爆表，市场整体情绪并不是非常乐观。

俄罗斯增加柴油供应的预期，让布油从周一的106美元上方回到105美元附近，十年期美债收益率也有所回落。油价降下来，有助于缓解后续通胀的担忧，收益率回落也能减轻股票的估值压力。不过现在布油仍然在100美元以上，沙特和霍尔木兹的安全问题还在，企业和居民面对的能源成本依然不低。

周三北京时间20点30分公布美国9月 CPI，市场预期整体同比3.7%，核心同比2.5%。通胀比上个月高，已经在市场预期之内，影响短期行情的是实际数据与预期的差距，尤其是其他商品和服务的价格有没有继续上涨。

如果数据低于预期，尤其是核心通胀没有预想中那么高，市场对继续加息的担忧可能缓和，科技股和 Bitcoin 也更容易延续反弹。如果只是符合预期，资金还会继续看油价和企业财报，如果明显高于预期，高利率维持更久的担忧又会增加，今天反弹的部分也容易回吐。

text:
Today we're sharing some initial data on how Americans use Claude for politics, based on aggregated conversation data analyzed with differentially private methods. A couple interesting takeaways:

*Almost no one asks AI how they should vote* 

About ~5.75% of conversations in the US touch on some kind of political or social issue in a recent one-week period, and less than 0.01% of conversations involve asking how to vote. 

*Political conversations have many goals*

These conversations have wide-ranging goals, everything from research and writing assistance to learning, fact-checking, and arguing. 

We are continuing to make progress on improving how Claude talks about these topics---steadily increasing our performance on our even-handedness evals and partnering with a range of outside organizations to develop new measures of political bias---and I hope that sharing information about the shape of these conversations will help people outside the company evaluate AI's political bias, accuracy, and other criteria in ecologically valid ways. I'd love to discuss this with people who are interested, as it was a huge priority for me before joining. 

This was a big joint effort as part of our work preparing for the midterm elections @AnthropicAI.

- 100–120g of protein daily 
- Meat at lunch & dinner 
- Vegetables at every meal
- Fruit 3x a day (kiwi is apparently good for baby's brain)
- Full-fat dairy and healthy fats
- Walnuts 
- Parmesan cheese 
- Fish 1x a week for omega-3s
- Kimchi in my third trimester for baby's gut 
- Little to no ultra-processed food (after first tri) 
- Prenatal vitamins

I had never been more motivated to body and brain build in my life.

text:
a quick rundown on what $PRL actually is now that it's live on Entropy and why there's so much hype around the ticker.

Pearl is the ultimate liquidity bait, where the devs cleverly mashed together the two fattest bubbles: crypto and AI infrastructure.

mechanically, it's an L1 blockchain running on Proof-of-Useful-Work consensus.

instead of burning electricity on pointless hash grinding like Bitcoin, the network forces GPUs to compute matrix multiplication (MatMul) - the baseline math that powers the training and inference of all neural networks.

the compute results are wrapped in ZK-proofs, allowing the blockchain to cheaply verify the work without needing to recompute everything from scratch.

the market is drooling over this right now for two reasons:

1. a "2 in 1" model for data centers. Hardware can handle commercial AI workloads and simultaneously use those exact same calculations to mine PRL, offsetting infrastructure costs in the process.

2. lack of venues. Retail is eating up the "AI mining" narrative, but perp venues with decent liquidity for this asset straight-up didn't exist until today.

whether this tech pays off in the long run or not - as traders, we couldn't care less. What matters is that it's flawlessly packaged hype.

retail sees the "AI + GPU + crypto" combo and is ready to ape into the ticker at any price.

rolling out a $PRL perp with 3x leverage ahead of sluggish CEXs is a strong move from Entropy.

the ability to trade the season's biggest AI narrative is guaranteed to pull massive trading volume and the first cascades of retail liquidations straight over here.
