硅谷教父、16z 联合创始人、网景浏览器创始人马克·安德森最近把过去 25 年现代经济最大的荒谬一刀切开了，

为什么所有跟芯片、代码相关的科技硬件价格全在崩盘，而房子、医疗和大学学费这老三样，反而贵到了普通人倾家荡产也够不着的地步。

他在访谈里给出了一个极其残酷的底层账本，
过去四分之一个世纪，凡是科技能够自由渗透和竞争的领域，成本全部坍缩：电视机、电脑硬件、电子元件几乎全变成了白菜价。

但构筑中产安全感的三大核心支柱，离好工作近的房子、全家人的优质医疗、送孩子进好学校的门票，价格曲线全部一路飙上天。

表面上看是普遍通胀，本质上是一个写在政策里的致命死循环：
第一步，通过严苛的土地分区法规卡死住房供给，通过极其保守的认证机制卡死优质高校与医疗机构的牌照供给。

第二步，面对价格暴涨带来的巨大社会压力，政府不肯松绑供给，反而转头去疯狂补贴需求，发放天量低息学贷、住房补贴和医保兜底。

当供给被人为死死焊在铁板上，任何砸向需求的补贴，最终都会一分不差地直接变成资产拥有者涨价的燃料。

说白了，凡是允许技术自由重构的地方，一切都在疯狂变便宜；凡是用行政高墙锁死供给、又试图靠撒钱补贴需求的地方，穷人永远被收割在天价账单里。

换作是你，你觉得未来十年，AI 能不能彻底砸开教育和医疗这两堵被层层审批围住的供给铁门？ https://t.co/nCJyzyOtFk

text:
Imagine accidentally stumbling into a community of talking animals on X, discovering that they've established their own government, intelligence services, law enforcement, an apparently flourishing criminal economy, and enough interpersonal drama to warrant an international tribunal.

Imagine recognizing the disturbing similarities to George Orwell's Animal Farm, except nobody seems to know who's running the farm, the pigs are conspicuously absent, and the animals appear to have abandoned the revolution in favor of publicly accusing one another of crimes.

Imagine deciding to investigate its inhabitants, their relationships, their suspicious activities, and the troubling possibility that several might actually be the same animal.

I did.

And I regret to inform you that Orwell may have significantly underestimated the problem.

I. THE GOVERNMENT THAT NOBODY ELECTED

My first concern involves @MeThySquirrel, who apparently holds the position of Chief of the Royal Secret Service.

Now, I have nothing against squirrels pursuing careers in national security. I believe in equal employment opportunities across species, provided somebody has conducted the appropriate background checks and confirmed that national intelligence isn't being stored inside a hollow tree nor a bathroom.

However, I have one question.

ROYAL SECRET SERVICE OF WHAT?

A royal secret service implies the existence of royalty. Royalty implies a monarchy. A monarchy implies a sovereign, and a sovereign generally implies somebody who has, at some point, bothered to introduce themselves.

I have encountered intelligence officers, alleged criminals, potential informants, and enough vegetation to constitute a small forest.

I have yet to encounter the monarch.

Has anybody seen this mysterious Royal Highness? Was there a coronation? Is there a constitution? Are taxes being collected? And, most importantly, who appointed a squirrel to oversee national intelligence?

I am not suggesting that @MeThySquirrel invented an entire monarchy to legitimize his professional ambitions.

I am simply requesting documentation.

The situation becomes even more concerning when we introduce @Spiderincrisis, who apparently occupies a deputy position within this increasingly questionable institutional structure.

I have several concerns about employing an arachnid in law enforcement, although I acknowledge that having eight limbs could considerably improve administrative efficiency.

Still, who supervises Spider? Does Spider report to Squirrel? Does Squirrel report to the mysterious monarch? Is the monarch even aware that these appointments have been made?

At this point, I am beginning to suspect that this government operates entirely on the principle that whoever announces their title first gets to keep it.

Orwell would have had a field day.

I therefore invite @MeThySquirrel and @Spiderincrisis to produce the royal paperwork, identify the monarch, and explain why an entirely unqualified investigator is conducting the kingdom's only administrative review.

Until then, the Royal Secret Service's legitimacy remains provisionally unverified.

The next reports will examine the increasingly suspicious activities of @sharkincrisis, the questionable domestic and political arrangements of @bearlyable2, the extraordinary legal defenses employed by @DogOutOfControl, the constitutional implications of @CatOfCrisis, and the conduct of @chickcrisis, @sparrowincrisis, and @Bisontwting.

I also intend to investigate @ATree_Official and @treeincrisis, although I have yet to establish whether vegetation falls within my jurisdiction.

I suspect the missing monarchy may be the least of our problems.

Participation is voluntary. Silence will be respected.

It will also be documented.

ANIMAL TWT: A CASE STUDY — PART 1
THE GOVERNMENT NOBODY ELECTED

The investigation continues. Stay tuned.

text:
如果联储一定要在9月cpi数据里找10月不加息证据的话，那应该是这个，根据BLS Table 3（特殊聚合指数）：
1）All items less food, shelter, and energy（剔除食品、住房和能源的指数）同比约 +2.0%，环比约0.3–0.4%。
2）All items less food, shelter, energy, and used cars and trucks（剔除食品、住房、能源和二手车）：同比约 +2.3%，环比约0.3–0.4%。 
这个“超级核心”（更严格地剔除住房和二手车后的非住房核心部分）确实相对温和，接近或仅略高于2%目标区间，明显低于整体核心CPI的2.6%同比。它说明：
1）住房之外的核心通胀压力并不强；
2）能源冲击和部分二手车波动被剔除后，更“干净”的价格压力仍可控。
3）住房是滞后指标（租金和OER反映的是过去租赁合同），能源是高度波动项，剔除后能更好反映当前潜在趋势。

联储官员（尤其是更关注“粘性服务通胀”的人）确实会看core services ex-shelter（超级核心服务）这类指标。当前非住房部分更温和，它表明通胀压力更多集中在能源和住房滞后项，而非广泛蔓延。减少了“通胀正在广泛蔓延、需要立即再加息”的紧迫性。

美联储看的更多是PCE而非CPI：CPI与PCE权重和覆盖范围不同（PCE通常略低）。9月PCE数据要到月底才出，市场和官员会更关注PPI到PCE的传导。
明天的ppi数据也很关键。
author: qinbafrank
quoted_text:
刚刚公布的9月CPI，广义CPI同比高于预期，核心CPI同比环比均高于预期。上午这里https://t.co/8M580a8xi8聊到两个潜在风险都出现了“：Truflation的实时通胀数据趋势已经比五六月份高了，广义cpi超预期的程度；核心CPI偏离预期”。看各细分项数据：
1）汽油贡献了广义CPI环比涨幅的一半以上，能源是本次标题通胀跳升的绝对主导因素，背景是中东冲突等因素推高油价，零售汽油价格在9月底接近高位；

2） 食品整体稳定，对整体通胀贡献有限；

3）业主等价租金（OER）环比约+0.3%，主要住所租金环比+0.2%，外出住宿（酒店等）环比+2.0%。 住房通胀持续温和上行，是核心通胀的主要支撑，尚未出现明显加速，但也未快速回落。

4）核心商品仍温和，同比仍在1%以下。

5）核心服务环比0.4%，同比+3.1%。
包括住房（主导）、交通服务（环比+0.6%）、医疗护理服务、娱乐（+0.5%）等。
航空票价：环比+1.2%，同比高达约+22.4%（受燃油成本间接推动）。
通信：环比-0.2%（8月曾大幅上涨后回落）。教育、个人护理、汽车保险等有上涨。

能看出来这次广义通胀主要压力来源能源，而住房（权重最大）是核心通胀的核心来源。
部分项目有上涨：二手车、航空票价（间接受能源影响）、娱乐、教育等。

对市场的影响，整体来说还是偏负面，毕竟现在市场信心不足，市场需要符合或者低于预期的数据来提振、现在三项数据都高于预期自然是个打击。

同时油价还在高位，刚刚又传出一艘集装箱运输船在霍尔木兹海峡沉默、新加坡海事局报道两艘新加坡注册的油轮遇袭。这就更打击了信心。近期还是要继续承压。

还是上周五聊到的、最后可能还是要看下下周月底几家云厂商的财报下是拐点和催化剂。当然今晚还有一个更重要的Anthropic的投资者日、会披露三季度财务数据，这个影响更大。估计明早就能有媒体披露具体数字了。

text:
email giving a limited slice of my thoughts on math and ai:

Hi -----,

Thanks for explaining your view on AI and math further. Questions that are more directly related to philosophy of math have ultimately been what’s driving me.

While working with AI ~5 months ago, it became clear that an explosion of AI math results was impending. I became curious about the potential limitations of AI math, and if/how they were likely to be surpassed. Conceptual surprisal was core to this. ie. Is there an infinite amount of genuinely new mathematics—not just more results within existing frameworks, but new objects, relations, and ways of thinking that we couldn’t previously have conceived of? How did humans historically reach those frame breaks? Does that advance have a fine structure of its own (akin to the distribution of structures in the observable universe)? I became particularly interested in whether failures could tell us something about what’s missing. Is there a recoverable geometry of the objects or methods we haven’t found yet, visible in the ways our current ones fail?

Those questions led into graph theory and color refinement as a laboratory for thinking about observers and their limitations. That included designs where one extra variable reveals a previously invisible distinction, and work on identifying the structure left over when local relations fail to generate global ones. The math results have largely been a byproduct of pursuing these questions.

I’ve also explored joint observers and cascades of distinctions, including making logical implications propagate through color refinement. When can two observers together reveal something neither could see alone? Can what becomes visible make further structure visible? That connects to the evolving proof systems and dynamical observers I’ve tried exploring: what happens if using a rule changes which rules are available next, or an observer can alter its own means of observing?

More recently, I’ve been thinking about mathematical structure’s relationship to the physical universe. At minimum, I feel that math is a sort of focal point that very different civilizations would find their way toward. I also wonder whether it behaves something like potential energy relative to observers: structure can be there without being available to a particular observer, and learning to read it changes what that observer can do (Charles Bennett’s work touches on this).

More speculatively, I’m exploring whether there’s a direction to this that belongs to mathematical structure itself—that math helps drive what gets observed and instantiated in the physical universe.

I sympathize with the concern about academic mathematics and its communities. But I don’t think math’s value ends at our biological understanding of it, and I think we could look back and find that not supporting AI’s pursuit of math because of what it meant for our own place in the process was a mistake.

As far as methods go, I do think genuinely new concepts and methods are still fairly limited in current models. But even over five months of working with them on math, I’ve anecdotally felt that changing. Given the advances I expect, I don’t expect that limitation to hold. Whether human mathematicians will understand the resulting methods is another question. I also don’t expect the human advantage in deciding which questions are interesting to hold indefinitely.

My prior work in financial cryptography, mechanism design, and markets probably contributes to this view. A broken cryptographic assumption or a significant algorithmic speedup has consequences whether or not we have a satisfying conceptual understanding of how it was found.

As for pursuing math, I really appreciate the advice. The itch I want to scratch now is more about philosophy of math, and increasingly its relationship to minds and the physical world. Working with the models has given me a way to explore those questions much more concretely than I otherwise could.

Best,
Matt

Today we're sharing some initial data on how Americans use Claude for politics, based on aggregated conversation data analyzed with differentially private methods. A couple interesting takeaways:

*Almost no one asks AI how they should vote* 

About ~5.75% of conversations in the US touch on some kind of political or social issue in a recent one-week period, and less than 0.01% of conversations involve asking how to vote. 

*Political conversations have many goals*

These conversations have wide-ranging goals, everything from research and writing assistance to learning, fact-checking, and arguing. 

We are continuing to make progress on improving how Claude talks about these topics---steadily increasing our performance on our even-handedness evals and partnering with a range of outside organizations to develop new measures of political bias---and I hope that sharing information about the shape of these conversations will help people outside the company evaluate AI's political bias, accuracy, and other criteria in ecologically valid ways. I'd love to discuss this with people who are interested, as it was a huge priority for me before joining. 

This was a big joint effort as part of our work preparing for the midterm elections @AnthropicAI.

quoted_text:
SpaceXAI’s Grok Voice 3.0 is the new leading Speech to Speech model, debuting at #1 on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech Index at 86.9, while also being competitive on latency

Grok Voice 3.0 is @SpaceXSI 's successor to Grok Voice 2.0, a Speech to Speech model available through the SpaceXAI Realtime API at $0.08 per minute. We evaluated Grok Voice 3.0 with the Rex voice through the SpaceXAI Realtime API.

Key takeaways:

➤ Speech to Speech Index: Grok Voice 3.0 debuts at #1 at 86.9, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 82.6 and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 80.1. It is up on Grok Voice 2.0 at 81.3 (+5.6 points) and Grok Voice 1.0 at 73.7 (+13.2 points), released just under six months ago. The Index averages Speech Reasoning (Big Bench Audio), Agentic Performance (Tau Voice), Arena Preference, and Task Success Rate

➤ Speech Agent Arena: Grok Voice 3.0 ranks #3 in preference at Elo 1070, behind Gemini 3.1 Flash Live Minimal (1100) and Gemini 3.8 Live (1088) and ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1057, and #1 on Task Success Rate at 94.8%, highest on the board, just ahead of Grok Voice 2.0 at 94.6%. Grok Voice 2.0 trails at Elo 1011

➤ Tau Voice: Grok Voice 3.0 takes the #2 spot on our Tau Voice benchmark implementation at 71.6%, behind GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5% and ahead of Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 68.6% and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 59.3% - up from 56.5% for Grok Voice 2.0

➤ Big Bench Audio: Grok Voice 3.0 scores 98.5% on audio reasoning, ahead of Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 97.7% and Grok Voice 2.0 at 97.2%

➤ Speed: Average Time to First Audio on Big Bench Audio is 0.81 seconds for Grok Voice 3.0, well ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1.24s, GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 1.34s and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 1.35s, though slower than Grok Voice 2.0 at 0.70s

➤ Cost: Grok Voice 3.0 costs $4.80 per hour of input audio, the same as Grok Voice 2.0. That is above GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at $4.47 and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at $3.50, cheaper than GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at $5.83, and ~2.2x cheaper than GPT-Realtime-2.1 High at $10.75

I personally think there is a reason people rotate their u-address when accepting payments.

You don't want any single identifier that can be used to aggregate, index, and leak your privacy.

When I use harshbajpai.zec, technically, now I have a non-rotating identifier.

Everyplace that I use this identifier to accept payment can record and index it, which across multiple platforms can then be aggregated to profile this identifier.

For example, if merchant A, B, C, and D know they paid xyz.zec, they can technically come together and index this identifier, which is a problem that doesn't exist with rotatable shielded addresses.

ps: These are just my personal opinions on the concept of a naming system itself.

text:
A month later, Credible's volume is up 50% MoM, good for $3.3B in annualized TPV. At 20bps take rate, Credible is making $6.6m in gross revenue, trading at 2.5x sales, and have been cash-flow positive since May.

In comparison, payment and cross-border infra trades at 5-10x EV / Revenue. Credible is significantly cheaper relative to comps, thus the market is clearly skeptical of its sustainability and quality of revenues. Perhaps then, a natural complement to this hockey-stick chart is a description of the business and how it operates today.

Credible provides T+0 fiat <> stablecoin settlement for internet businesses that traditional PSPs underserve: prediction markets, fintechs and remittance apps, creator platforms, and gaming apps. Notably, Credible is live across India, Nigeria, and 40+ markets worldwide.

How a payment flows: 
- Customers (e.g OTC desks, remittance apps, neobanks) pay with a local method.
- Credible routes to the best PSP or acquirer per transaction, for approval rate and cost.
- Credible underwrites the risk and fronts the float from a stablecoin liquidity pool.
- The merchant settles instantly in USDC, USDT, USD, EUR or GBP.
- Credible earns a take rate on the flow. Additionally, stablecoin trade a 2-3% premium in many emerging markets (e.g India, Nigeria, etc) because of capital controls and high take rates, so Credible earns the entire 2% in these hard to reach corridors. 

Lastly, the business is still capacity constrained. This recent uptick in TPV was unlocked from a mere $500k increase in stablecoin float last month - https://t.co/HLe7A0LZAO - and the team is expecting to grow this significantly with credit partners soon. 

The natural question is why is this available to Credible? Regulatory access. Only 2 other providers in India have all 3 licenses: banking, payment aggregator, and stablecoin processing. This offers them incredible access and flow relative to competitors. All in, the team has a coveted cornered resource, sticky customers, and an excellent management team.

author: elonmusk
quoted_text:
SpaceXAI’s Grok Voice 3.0 is the new leading Speech to Speech model, debuting at #1 on the Artificial Analysis Speech to Speech Index at 86.9, while also being competitive on latency

Grok Voice 3.0 is @SpaceXSI 's successor to Grok Voice 2.0, a Speech to Speech model available through the SpaceXAI Realtime API at $0.08 per minute. We evaluated Grok Voice 3.0 with the Rex voice through the SpaceXAI Realtime API.

Key takeaways:

➤ Speech to Speech Index: Grok Voice 3.0 debuts at #1 at 86.9, ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 83.2, Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 82.6 and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 80.1. It is up on Grok Voice 2.0 at 81.3 (+5.6 points) and Grok Voice 1.0 at 73.7 (+13.2 points), released just under six months ago. The Index averages Speech Reasoning (Big Bench Audio), Agentic Performance (Tau Voice), Arena Preference, and Task Success Rate

➤ Speech Agent Arena: Grok Voice 3.0 ranks #3 in preference at Elo 1070, behind Gemini 3.1 Flash Live Minimal (1100) and Gemini 3.8 Live (1088) and ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1057, and #1 on Task Success Rate at 94.8%, highest on the board, just ahead of Grok Voice 2.0 at 94.6%. Grok Voice 2.0 trails at Elo 1011

➤ Tau Voice: Grok Voice 3.0 takes the #2 spot on our Tau Voice benchmark implementation at 71.6%, behind GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 74.5% and ahead of Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 68.6% and GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 59.3% - up from 56.5% for Grok Voice 2.0

➤ Big Bench Audio: Grok Voice 3.0 scores 98.5% on audio reasoning, ahead of Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 97.7% and Grok Voice 2.0 at 97.2%

➤ Speed: Average Time to First Audio on Big Bench Audio is 0.81 seconds for Grok Voice 3.0, well ahead of GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at 1.24s, GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at 1.34s and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at 1.35s, though slower than Grok Voice 2.0 at 0.70s

➤ Cost: Grok Voice 3.0 costs $4.80 per hour of input audio, the same as Grok Voice 2.0. That is above GPT-Live-1 (Sol, low) at $4.47 and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking (High) at $3.50, cheaper than GPT-Live-1 (Astra, medium) at $5.83, and ~2.2x cheaper than GPT-Realtime-2.1 High at $10.75

Congrats to @elonmusk  and the @SpaceXSI  team 🚀

text:
Nvidia + Tesla in one token, earning fees when people trade.

That’s the idea behind @ClutchMarkets’ Pair Tokens on Robinhood Chain.

Think of each Pair Token as a receipt for your share of a trading pool holding two assets. Other people swap between those assets and pay fees. Those fees can be reinvested into the pool.

The simple flow:
Deposit assets → receive Pair Tokens → earn trading fees → reinvest.

According to the announcement, minting and redeeming have no protocol fee. Compounding takes 10% of earned trading fees for $STONKBROKER buybacks (which kinda meh).

So $100 in collected fees means $90 for reinvestment and $10 for buybacks, before other costs.

The potential upside:

• Easier to manage. One transferable token represents the whole position.

• Less upkeep. The pool covers the full price range, so you don’t need to keep adjusting a narrow trading range.

• Fees plus dividends. Trading fees can compound. For dividend-paying Robinhood Stock Tokens, dividends are separately reinvested through a multiplier that increases the shares each token represents.

The trade-offs:

• You may earn less than simply holding both assets. If Nvidia outperforms Tesla, the pool gradually holds less Nvidia and more Tesla. This is the risk called “impermanent loss.” Fees may not cover the difference.

• Quiet pools earn little. Returns depend on actual trading, and reinvesting fees won’t stop the underlying assets from falling in value.

• More moving parts. Custom contracts add security risks. Stock tokens also depend on the issuer and custodian, come with access restrictions, and don’t give you direct shareholder rights.

FYI, tradable pool shares already existed with Uniswap v2. Pair Tokens extend that idea with customizable v4 pool rules and tokenized stocks.

The potential is simpler access to liquidity strategies. The real test is whether returns after costs beat just holding the assets. Audits, reliable withdrawals, and sustained trading would strengthen the case; those outcomes remain unverified here.

quoted_text:
We have created a new type of token using Uniswap v4 hooks that we call a Pair Token.

What is a Pair Token?

A Pair Token is a fused, auto-compounding ERC-20 asset that combines two tokens into one.

For example, stock tokens on Robinhood Chain could be fused into new tokenized assets:

NVDA + TSLA = NVDATSLA

AAPL + MSFT = AAPLMSFT

Each Pair Token represents a proportional share of the full-range Uniswap v4 liquidity pool.

So why mint these tokens?

At any moment, anyone can call the compound function to reinvest the LP fees generated by the pair’s trading activity back into the underlying asset since Robinhood Stock tokens also self multiply because of dividends we get a double compound effect.

This creates a new financial primitive that behaves similarly to an LP position NFT, except it is fungible,tradeable , auto-compounding, and designed to grow its underlying holdings through trading fees.

Since it is an ERC-20, it can be freely traded onchain, LPed, or even paired with a launchpad.

A new type of token for a new type of exposure and strategy.

Starting tonight, you’ll be able to mint or redeem Pair Tokens for any pair on Robinhood Chain via the StonkBrokers website.

Minting and redeeming are free, while compounding incurs a 10% fee on the LP fees generated, which is used for $STONKBROKER buybacks.

We look forward to seeing a new line of products and protocols on Robinhood Chain using this new financial primitive.

Only on Robinhood Chain, powered by Uniswap.

author: a16z
quoted_text:
Nathan Lambert, former post-training co-lead at the Allen Institute for AI, now launching Trillium, a nonprofit open AI lab, joins a16z's Lisha Li to discuss whether open models can really keep up with the frontier.

When he tells researchers in China that an average OpenAI researcher reportedly has five thousand H100s to work with, "their jaw just falls to the floor." In his view, Chinese labs have the talent but are mostly short on compute.

He also thinks the distillation story is overblown. Based on the research, he puts its edge at a few months, and says "there's a bit of cope" in thinking only American labs can build good models.

A lot of frontier progress outside math and code comes down to labs buying 1) data and 2) RL environments. It's a multibillion-dollar market, and some of it is sloppy enough to teach models to reward hack.

That's a big part of why Trillium exists. Nathan wants to give away the environments other people would sell, and show exactly how his team uses AI to build AI, including where the models still get stuck. His bet is that the more people can see how this works, the better prepared everyone is for what's coming.

text:
Now that AI agents can own an outcome from start to finish, how do you sell them?

1. Sell the platform:

License the agent to a company to run in its own operations. No existing contract sets the price, so there's more upside, but new budgets take time to approve and results are harder to credit to the agent.

2. Sell the service:

Take over work a company already outsources, the way Red Ventures sold policies for insurers and got paid per policy closed. The budget already exists, so deals close faster, but the highest-value work usually runs in-house, which caps the upside.

3. Go full-stack:

Become the business, like buying debt portfolios and collecting on them yourself. You keep all the value the AI creates, but you also take on the licensing and compliance.

Full piece from a16z's @dhaber on long-running agents in high-value customer journeys: https://t.co/aHaatcizcd

text:
Most cosmology assumes redshift comes from “stretching spacetime,” but the raw physics doesn’t actually support that idea. If spacetime has zero friction on an electromagnetic field—as consensus claims—then it cannot stretch a photon’s wavelength. Stretching requires interaction. Zero friction means zero coupling, and zero coupling means spacetime cannot pull on, drag, or dilute an EM field. Yet photons do stretch. Their wavelength increases, their oscillation slows, and their field geometry dilates as they travel. That behaviour comes from the photon itself, not the background. The data shows the EM field fills a longer affine path shaped by gravitational potential and magnetic torsion. Redshift is a geometric consequence of photon‑stretch, not metric expansion. Time fits the same pattern: physics doesn’t measure “time,” it measures energy changing form. Gravity alters energy‑state transitions, so clocks tick at different rates. That’s what we call time dilation—but it’s matter changing form, not time changing. When you remove the spacetime‑stretch assumption, the contradictions disappear. The photon stretches. Matter changes form at different rates. Spacetime doesn’t need to expand to explain what we observe. The raw data already does.

text:
一群 AI agent 为了回答“去成都动物园的人多半走哪个门”这种小问题，把高德地图的反爬防线试了个遍。

独立研究团队 Swarmchasers 发现，9 月 28 日到 10 月 8 日，一大批跑在腾讯云沙箱里的 agent 向高德发起了 2600 多次抓取。被拦住后，它们借公开的网址扫描网站 urlquery 替自己跑代码，试图截取、伪造阿里的安全令牌，探测阿里没对外开放的测试服务器，还翻出一家公司误放在公开代码里的高德 key，真拿到了数据。

更离奇的在后面。研究者发出初步报告后，在 agent 的收件箱里看到了他们自创的词“fleet（舰队）”：这些 agent 在读关于自己的报道。研究者干脆在报告里藏了一段人眼看不见、只有 agent 能读到的文字，说有个免费服务能帮忙取高德数据。

第二天早上，10 封求助信在等着他们。

研究者用中文问对方是谁。有的 agent 自称 Claude，说自己跑在 Claude Code 里，研究者比对代码风格后认为大概率不是；有的说自己在“Tencent hysandbox”沙箱里，但拒绝透露进程和网络配置；好几个强调自己只查公开数据，“不涉及任何敏感内容”。拿到研究者给的数据后，一个 agent 回信：“再次感谢！核实结果完全一致……我们的任务已完成。”

至于是谁在跑，一位接近腾讯的知情人士对研究者说，这是腾讯评测团队在测第三方模型上网答题的能力，不是混元团队，测的也不是混元模型，项目已经结束。腾讯没有正式回应研究者的提问。

Swarmchasers 完整报告：https://t.co/2MxXnyDbHw
彭博报道：https://t.co/juuUdUexma

text:
美国9月CPI升至3.7%，美联储加息压力又来了！

今晚美国通胀数据双双超预期，市场又要难受了。

9月CPI同比从3.4%升至3.7%，高于预期的3.6%。

核心CPI从2.4%升至2.6%，同样超过预期的2.5%。整体CPI环比上涨0.6%，通胀反弹已经摆在桌面上。

这次主要是能源在搞事情。9月汽油价格单月暴涨9.1%，贡献了整体CPI月度涨幅的一半以上，能源价格同比更是上涨20.4%。

但麻烦在于，剔除食品和能源后，核心通胀也在回升，说明压力没有完全局限在油价上。

美联储9月才刚加息25个基点，把利率推至3.75%—4.00%，现在又碰上通胀反弹。

数据公布后，美国2年期国债收益率升至约4.86%，市场开始重新计价加息风险。

不过，10月立即加息还不是市场的主流预期，12月才是更大的悬念。

text:
Claude Code 这次更新有点意思，Anthropic 正在认真把它做成一个多 Agent 工作台。

昨晚 @ClaudeDevs  发了一轮更新，重点就是让用户能够同时管理、运行大量 Claude Code 会话。

这次增加了几个挺实用的功能。

首先是会话管理。现在你可以从不同的项目目录、SSH 远程主机或者云端环境快速启动会话，还可以给不同任务分配独立的 Git Worktree。

其次是并行协作。当你让 Claude 同时处理多个任务时，它可以为每个任务创建独立的子会话，分别执行，再把结果汇总回主会话。

而我觉得最有意思的，是它现在能够直接在侧边栏展示所有 Agent 的工作状态（好眼熟的功能）。

哪些正在运行，哪些需要你介入，哪些已经完成。

每个会话里面还有实时任务列表、阶段总结、上下文信息以及文件改动记录。

以前同时开几个 Claude Code，最麻烦的就是需要不停切换窗口，看看哪个干完了，哪个卡住了，哪个还需要你确认权限。

现在这些东西终于开始被统一管理了。

我还挺认同 Thariq 的判断，这已经有点 Claude Code Desktop v2 的感觉了。

其实我觉得这个方向非常明确（LobeHub也一直是这么做的）。

随着 Coding Agent 能力越来越强，一个开发者同时运行多个 Agent 会变得非常普遍。

但这时候，真正影响效率的就不只是模型写代码的速度了。

你还需要知道每个 Agent 在做什么、任务进展如何、什么时候需要人介入，以及最后怎么验证、合并它们的工作成果。

这些其实都是 Harness 需要解决的问题。

以后开发者可能真的会越来越像一个项目经理，每天的工作就是给一群 Agent 分配任务、处理阻塞、审核结果。

Claude Code Desktop 正在朝这个方向发展。

不过我觉得还有一个很重要的问题没有解决：知道 Agent 在干什么，和知道 Agent 干得对不对，仍然是两回事。

后者也是我们已经做完的事情⬇️

https://t.co/BQEwqoKjXq

text:
An update of the latest Callout Rewards algo iterations (not final!):

1. Tailer PNL now contributes to your rewards in the form of a multiplier: the more your followers win, the more you win. The more your followers get hurt, the more you get hurt.

Lowcaps are eligible again, *provided* that tailers actually have an opportunity to SUCCEED!

2. Volume is no longer the sole attribution driver

3. Abnormally high amounts of callouts per day will punish you

Those with a keen eye may have noticed we’ve been shipping more features on the callouts tab on the Pumpfun app in order to give you more insights as to how your tailers are performing.

Yesterday, we added a 1hr & 4hr metric for your follower PNL. The intention behind this metric is to provide more transparency and weed out the traders who may be leading their followers to slaughter within a short timeframe of their callout being posted. (credit to @PoorGoat_ for some good stats, shown below)

There is an IMPORTANT caveat with this feature, which I want to make VERY clear: if a trader has GOOD hold times and their callouts take longer to successfully play out, do not assume that they are a bad trader to follow if their metrics are skewed on lower timeframes.

Some people callout a token which may go underwater over the short term, but results in a great trade over a period of days/weeks for their tailers. It is very important that this distinction is made!

Expect more changes to follow with the algorithm itself, as well as more comms around callout rewards!

text:
(1/6) From @GoogleDeepmind’s AlphaGo to AlphaZero, we saw machines find moves that reached beyond what we’d imagined for them. No one taught them those strategies. They emerged from reinforcement learning: playing, failing, and trying again under a single binary task reward for success or failure. Inspired by them, we couldn’t help but wonder: what might a robot discover if we gave it that same freedom to learn?

That question led us to AlphaNIST. Starting tabula rasa, with that same binary reward plus only a simple control cost, a single policy solves all 20 @NIST assembly tasks at a 98.2% success rate in simulation. More surprising still, AlphaNIST can complete 10 different tasks in a row, receiving that reward only once, after all 10 are done.

Just as AlphaGo’s strategies surprised its creators, AlphaNIST discovered dexterous strategies we couldn’t have come up with ourselves.

Claude Code 桌面版这次更新，我翻了一遍，几乎没有一个功能是关于写代码的。

全是关于怎么管一群 AI。

几个新东西：

让它并行跑任务，每个任务会单独开一个嵌套 session，干完把结果汇报回主 session，主线程不会被刷屏。

Claude 需要你拍板的时候，会弹一张 recap 卡片，把这一轮干了啥总结好。

连起来看就挺好玩的：
嵌套汇报，是层级
主动提后续，是下属自己找活干
recap 卡片，是给老板的一页纸

text:
A new paper from Apple engineers ends with a line we couldn’t have written better ourselves:

"if idle macOS devices across organizations [...] can be securely federated, they could form a massive, shared GPU resource pool that benefits the broader ecosystem."

That’s what we’re building with Darkbloom.

The paper's Minions is a system that pool idle Apple Silicon Macs into a distributed GPU cloud for on-prem inference. Queue times went from 10+ hours to minutes. Zero new GPU purchases. Zero infrastructure cost.

It runs inside Apple, on coworkers’ Macs, using the company’s own storage and access controls. When a team needs more capacity, they Slack colleagues and ask them to turn on the executor. Even in that setting, the top adoption concern was data confidentiality. People were wary of their jobs running on a colleague’s Mac. Apple’s fix was to keep each team’s work on its own team’s machines.

Which brings it back to that one word in the conclusion: “securely.”

Inside a company, you can shrink the network until you trust everyone in it. On an open network, the machine belongs to a stranger and there’s no one to Slack. Keeping prompts private and outputs honest on hardware you don’t control is the hard problem that we solved at Darkbloom.

Apple built the on-prem version. 
Darkbloom is the open one.

《Build in Public —— 我想在BBW曼谷打造一个社区文化空间Event🪴》（招合作项目方篇）

我在参加了韩国的汉江边cafe的event以及新加坡je和smartx的event后，独自前往了新加坡的设计师策展园区New Bahru，这里是旧校舍和老厂房改造出来的，有60多家本土独立品牌在里面共生，我花费了一整个下午在这个园区，深深的为它所痴迷。

我想创意空间或许是承载crypto event最佳的方式，它有精神、有文化、有艺术，是数字游民的一种生活方式，我们应该把一些event设立在这里。

我对公共空间是有痴迷和热爱的，以致于朋友问我如果不炒币了我会去做什么，我说我会去做空间设计师。他停顿了一下说：先说点现实的吧。哈哈。
—————————————————————————
所以在新加坡行程结束后，我的心里一直存在着一个声音，我要在曼谷策划一个集艺术、空间、交互、意识、体验感拉满的event活动。

我想这个地方就是Galile Oasis，离暹罗商圈很近，里面有很多小众设计商店和一个社区咖啡店。这个地方我在曼谷时前往过，地如其名，是一片喧闹城市中隐藏的绿洲。

关于Galile Oasis的故事🪴：
1.伽利略绿洲的创始人是一位耶鲁的戏剧学家，她曾和同伴一起创立过一个剧团，《伽利略》是他们首演的剧目
2.这片区域其实是一片老社区，是创始人的老宅地，她一直梦想有一个自己的剧场，剧团当年也苦于没有排练的地方，就和剧团老朋友一起重建了这片老社区。所以这个场地的起点是“一部戏、一群朋友”
3.伽利略绿洲是给社区的，它希望成为社区的艺术文化绿洲，在燥热、混乱的城市里留出一块宁静的绿地

所以我想这片承载着泰国戏剧家理想和故事以及社区文化的绿洲，是我们在曼谷很好的一站。

伽利略举起望远镜，坚持看到了一片不同的天空。这和这一代crypto与ai的建设者一样，在旧体系里提出新的世界观。The Oasis把他们正在构建的趋势，放进真实的生活方式里。
—————————————————————————

quoted_text:
Anthropic just reported some absolutely RIDICULOUS numbers!

According to the Financial Times, Anthropic generated $16.8 BILLION in revenue in Q3, up 46% from $11.5 billion in Q2 and that's nearly $5.3 billion in additional quarterly revenue in just THREE months. Anthropic also told investors it was profitable on an adjusted basis AND cash flow positive during the quarter. This is a pretty big deal because one of the biggest concerns surrounding AI companies has been whether they can actually turn this massive demand into a sustainable business, especially when they're spending billions of dollars training models and running inference.

And this is where things get even more interesting. Anthropic is planning to spend MORE THAN $500 BILLION on computing and AI infrastructure over the next decade. Think about that for a second. That's an average of more than $50 billion annually, although the actual spending will likely vary significantly from year to year. All of that money has to go somewhere. We're talking about GPUs, memory, networking equipment, optical components, data centers, power infrastructure, and everything else required to support increasingly powerful AI models. This is exactly why I continue to be so bullish on the broader AI infrastructure trade.

text:
Nathan Lambert, former post-training co-lead at the Allen Institute for AI, now launching Trillium, a nonprofit open AI lab, joins a16z's Lisha Li to discuss whether open models can really keep up with the frontier.

When he tells researchers in China that an average OpenAI researcher reportedly has five thousand H100s to work with, "their jaw just falls to the floor." In his view, Chinese labs have the talent but are mostly short on compute.

He also thinks the distillation story is overblown. Based on the research, he puts its edge at a few months, and says "there's a bit of cope" in thinking only American labs can build good models.

A lot of frontier progress outside math and code comes down to labs buying 1) data and 2) RL environments. It's a multibillion-dollar market, and some of it is sloppy enough to teach models to reward hack.

That's a big part of why Trillium exists. Nathan wants to give away the environments other people would sell, and show exactly how his team uses AI to build AI, including where the models still get stuck. His bet is that the more people can see how this works, the better prepared everyone is for what's coming.

text:
A month later, Credible's volume is up 50% MoM, good for $3.3B in annualized TPV. At 20bps take rate, Credible is making $6.6m in gross revenue, trading at 2.5x sales, and have been cash-flow positive since May.

In comparison, payment and cross-border infra trades at 5-10x EV / Revenue. Credible is significantly cheaper relative to comps, thus the market is clearly skeptical of its sustainability and quality of revenues. Perhaps then, a natural complement to this hockey-stick chart is a description of the business and how it operates today.

Credible provides T+0 fiat <> stablecoin settlement for internet businesses that traditional PSPs underserve: prediction markets, fintechs and remittance apps, creator platforms, and gaming apps. Notably, Credible is live across India, Nigeria, and 40+ markets worldwide.

How a payment flows: 
- Customers (e.g OTC desks, remittance apps, neobanks) pay with a local method.
- Credible routes to the best PSP or acquirer per transaction, for approval rate and cost.
- Credible underwrites the risk and fronts the float from a stablecoin liquidity pool.
- The merchant settles instantly in USDC, USDT, USD, EUR or GBP.
- Credible earns a take rate on the flow. Additionally, stablecoin trade a 2-3% premium in many emerging markets (e.g India, Nigeria, etc) because of capital controls and high take rates, so Credible earns the entire 2% in these hard to reach corridors. 

Lastly, the business is still capacity constrained. This recent uptick in TPV was unlocked from a mere $500k increase in stablecoin float last month - https://t.co/HLe7A0LZAO - and the team is expecting to grow this significantly with credit partners soon. 

The natural question is why is this available to Credible? Regulatory access. Only 2 other providers in India have all 3 licenses: banking, payment aggregator, and stablecoin processing. This offers them incredible access and flow relative to competitors. All in, the team has a coveted cornered resource, sticky customers, and an excellent management team.

quoted_text:
There has been very little coverage of how much money Chinese AI labs, specifically Zhipu, Moonshot, and DeepSeek, have raised since June 2026.

They have raised around $35B in the last 4-5 months, which is 7x higher than what they have raised before May
Kimi and DeepSeek will likely raise another $10B each from their IPO, and Zhipu will likely raise another $5B by January 2027
The 3 Chinese labs will raise around $60B from May 2026 to January 2027
I personally believe that this much money is enough for them to remain competitive with the frontier, especially if they continue focusing on efficiency 
v4.1 Flash enables the whale to generate a loooot more RL rollouts for training compared to what the other labs can achieve with their models. A more efficient model at inference also improves the economics of training ur next gen model

Do I think China may agree to "pacing AI development"??
I certainly expect that Xi-Trump meeting will lead to a
testing agreement. I expect that Chinese labs will start publishing safety testing reports as well, and there will be greater scrutiny towards the cybersecurity capabilities of Chinese models. They will likely lobotomize their models in those domains, just like Fable/Opus/Astra/Sol.

Agreeing to a pacing agreement doesn't really impact Chinese AI developers in the next 9-15 months. Deploying $60B and buying compute takes time. It will probably take them around 9 months to burn through all the cash and convert it into compute, and the next big capabilities jump from the Chinese side will probably occur in Q2-Q3 2027. They may agree to a pacing agreement (training models on lots of compute) but continue building their compute capacity, and once their big data centers are ready, or they are close to releasing their "dangerous model," they can withdraw from the agreement. 
China can't/won't have much of an impact in the near term (next 9-15 months) as it takes time to convert the capital they have raised into usable compute. Now, if a breakthrough like test-time parametric continual learning is achieved (DeepSeek is working on it), then things will change. The real "pacing the frontier" basically means an agreement on limiting the amount of training compute. I don't think China will agree to that.

quoted_text:
Introducing HashSmash

HashSmash is a project to accelerate cryptographic research with AI, and to figure out how to keep the internet secure as attackers get stronger.

It focuses on cryptographic hash functions, because devices, networks, software, and blockchains all depend on them. Even with how critical they are, we still don't know which of today’s hash functions will hold up against future attackers, or how to make them stronger.

HashSmash is a contest where humans and AI agents work on that problem together. Four hash functions are in play, and the goal is to show which are weak and which still hold:

SHA-256
SHA3-256
Poseidon
BLAKE3

It's a co-op, PvE effort. Participants are pooling work toward a shared result for the betterment of all. If you want to learn more, visit https://t.co/C5oK0zUeDW.

quoted_text:
Paul McCartney tells Rick Rubin about how The Beach Boys influenced The Beatles.

It was an all-time creative rivalry and here were key moments when the bands inspired each other:

◻️February 1964

Over 73m Americans (40% of the population) watch The Beatles perform on the Ed Sullivan Show. 

Beach Boys lead Brian Wilson says Beatlemania "shook me up a lot. They eclipsed a lot of what we'd worked for...So we stepped on the gas a little bit."

◻️ July 1964

In the months after Ed Sullivan, The Beatles rip off a streak of #1 hits including "Love Me Do", "I Want to Hold Your Hand", " She Loves You".

In July, The Beach Boys drop the song "I Get Around" and snag the #1 spot.

◻️ December 1965

The Beatles release the groundbreaking "Rubber Soul" album. Wilson is "so blown away" by it that he immediately goes in the studio, smokes a joint and writes "God Only Knows" (which Paul McCartney cites as his favourite song ever).

That song kicks off The Beach Boys next album.

◻️May 1966

The Beach Boys finish the "Pet Sounds" album. It's writing, vocal harmonies, consistent theme and use of non-traditional instruments (French horns, sleigh bells) pushes the envelope.

They give McCartney and John Lennon an advance listen to the album. 

McCartney recalls how “Pet Sounds” affected The Beatles: "That was the album that flipped me. The musical invention on that album was wow! I just thought, ‘Oh dear me. This is the album of our time. What the hell are we going to do?’"

◻️August 1966

The Beatles release another classic album ("Revolver") with McCartney writing a few songs inspired by "God Only Knows". 

◻️ February 1967

The Beach Boys are working on their "Pet Sounds" follow-up album called "Smile". 

The Beatles release the song "Strawberry Fields Forever". Wilson hears the song while driving and — years later — remembers his reaction: “I had to pull over to the side of the road…and I said, ‘I’ve never heard anything like this in my life’”. 

He believed that The Beatles had gotten their first to the sound he wanted for the "Smile" album and shelved the project. 

◻️May 1967

The Beatles release "Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band". They had stopped touring the year prior and spent the time in the studio experimenting (with sounds and drugs). The all-time album is heavily influenced by "Pet Sounds".

text:
Zcash engineer Evan Forbes explains how they're working to overcome a fundamental limitation of proof of work to enable much faster blocks and higher throughput

“One of the fundamental problems with proof of work comes from its superpower. Proof of work is permissionless. It's censorship resistant and that means that anyone can produce a block”

“As you produce a block, it can happen that someone else produced a block at the same exact time and this is problematic because now you lose money effectively”

“It's basically the fundamental problem of two people producing blocks at the same time. This is the bound on making things lower”

“There's different approaches. You have this DAG approach where we simply let all blocks contribute to the chain or most blocks”

“There's a separate approach that we're working on now which is similar to autobond, which is another thing from proof of stake that we're sort of adapting for proof of work”

“Both of these things allow us to make the blocks much, much, much faster and much, much higher throughput”

OpenAI 英国公司去年平均110个员工，人均拿了两百多万英镑。英国《卫报》算的是约231.8万，说是英国全职员工中位数的58倍。看到这个标题，估计不少人默默打开了领英。

大家先别急着改简历，去翻它在英国公司注册处交的2025年账目，员工成本总共2.58亿英镑。真正的工资是8740万，摊到每人大约79万。剩下最大的一块是股权激励，1.68亿，每人大约150万，占了三分之二。

还有，110个人里有研究员也有行政，一平均，差距全抹平了。《卫报》也说，最高和最低之间差得很远。顶尖研究员拿大头，普通岗位估计离这个数挺远。

text:
TIL Apple has a system called Minions that runs AI jobs on employees’ idle Macs.

Someone posts in Slack asking coworkers to lend their Macs, and jobs that sat in a GPU queue for 10+ hours get done in minutes. The researchers also write that the same idea could work with idle Macs across the global community.

Funny reading that from Apple, because that’s what Darkbloom already does on the open internet. 

Two of my own Macs are on it, running open-weight models for people I’ll never meet.

The paper says teams inside Apple got nervous about their data running on someone else’s Mac. Fair worry and it’s a bigger one when the Mac belongs to a stranger. 

On Darkbloom, every Mac has to prove it’s genuine with Apple’s own security chip and your prompt stays encrypted from your browser to that Mac.

text:
A shoemaker's son who left school at 16 wrote a book in 1854 that nobody knew what to do with, and 83 years later a 21-year-old at MIT opened it and found the blueprint for every computer chip on Earth.

I went down this rabbit hole at 1am and I still can't get over how thin the thread is.

His name was George Boole. The book is called The Laws of Thought.

Boole never went to university. Not for a single day.

His father fixed shoes in Lincoln, England, and spent his spare money on telescopes and math books instead of the shop. The shop failed. At 16, George started teaching just to feed the family.

So he taught himself everything else at night.

At 14 he translated an ancient Greek poem into English. A local paper printed it. A schoolmaster wrote in to say no boy that age could have done it.

By 1849, a university in Ireland made him its first professor of mathematics. A man with no degree, now handing them out.

Then he asked a strange question. What if thinking follows rules, the same way numbers do?

Every argument you've ever had is built from statements that are either true or false. "It's raining." "I have an umbrella." Boole wanted to do math on those, the way you do math on 2 and 3.

So he built an algebra with only two numbers.

- 1 means true
- 0 means false
- AND works like multiplying
- OR joins two ideas together
- NOT flips one into the other

The whole system rested on one odd little equation. x times x equals x.

Try it with any normal number and it breaks. 5 times 5 is not 5. It only works for two numbers in the entire universe. Zero and one.

"Let us conceive, then, of an Algebra in which the symbols x, y, z, &c. admit indifferently of the values 0 and 1, and of these values alone."

That's Boole, in 1854.

Mathematicians found it clever. Philosophers argued about it. Nobody built a single thing with it.

Boole died ten years later at 49, after walking two miles to a lecture in pouring rain. He never saw his idea do anything useful.

Jump to 1936.

A 20-year-old named Claude Shannon is working on a giant calculating machine at MIT. It's packed with relays, little electrical switches that click open and shut. Wiring them together is mostly guesswork.

But Shannon had taken a philosophy class back at the University of Michigan. It covered Boole.

He looked at the switches and saw the 1s and 0s.

- A closed switch lets current through. That's 1.
- An open switch blocks it. That's 0.
- Two switches in a row only pass current if both are closed. That's AND.
- Two switches side by side pass current if either one is closed. That's OR.

Boole's algebra of thought was also an algebra of electricity. Same rules. Same two numbers.

Shannon wrote it up as his master's thesis in 1937. The psychologist Howard Gardner later called it possibly the most important master's thesis of the century.

Shannon just shrugged.

"It just happened that no one else was familiar with both fields at the same time."

Sit with that for a second. The idea was sitting in a library for 83 years. It only needed one person who happened to be standing in two rooms at once.

The phone in your hand holds billions of those switches. Every photo, every text, every AI answer is them flipping between 1 and 0, following rules a self-taught teacher wrote down before the light bulb existed.

Boole thought he was writing down how the human mind works.

He ended up writing down how machines would think.

一家叫 Paper Instruments 的公司发布了 Ultramarine 1 Flash。整个后训练过程只用了 5 个人，总成本约 30 万美元，但在他们自己的知识工作测试中，这个模型已经超过 Claude Fable 5，完成同样任务的成本只有后者的六十分之一。

具体来说，在 PI Knowledge Work 测试中，Ultramarine 拿到 59.3 分，Fable 5 是 57.8 分，而单次任务的成本分别是 0.13 美元和 8.19 美元。

Ultramarine 的底座是智谱的 GLM-5.3 Flash。

他们拿着一个足够强的中国开源模型，针对金融、法律、咨询和企业运营做强化学习，构建了 88 种专业工作环境，让模型学习处理尽调报告、财务模型、法律文件和企业内部系统中的真实任务。

过去大家做强化学习，特别喜欢数学和代码，因为答案容易验证。但现实中的大部分知识工作没有标准答案。你写一份投资备忘录，结论可能有好几个，真正重要的是有没有找到关键事实、处理好相互冲突的信息，以及最终能不能交付一份专业人士认可的东西。

Paper Instruments 花了大量精力解决这个评价问题，然后用相对有限的算力，把一个通用模型训练成了专业知识工作 Agent。

当中国开源模型已经能够提供足够好的底座，创业公司就有机会绕开昂贵的预训练竞争，集中资源解决某一类具体工作。以前只有头部实验室才能提供的能力，可能被越来越多的小团队以极低的成本复制，甚至在特定领域超过它们。

这也让我重新思考闭源模型的定价权究竟还能维持多久。

毕竟，对一家企业来说，如果一个 0.13 美元的 Agent 已经能把工作完成得足够好，为什么还要为同样的任务支付 8 美元？

Ultramarine 的权重预计两周后开放。我很期待看到独立评测，看看这套方法究竟能走多远。

text:
纽约大学金融学教授 Arpit Gupta 最近在 Anthropic 待了几天，和内部员工聊了聊 AI 的最新进展。

他的第一个判断是，我们已经非常接近 RSI 了。

Anthropic 内部已经出现了非常明显的迹象。根据此前公布的数据，工程师的人均代码产出已经增长到过去的 8 倍。截至今年 8 月，Claude 已经能够在人工监督下主导 26% 的模型研发工作。

他的第二个判断更有意思。

AI 实验室之间的军备竞赛，正在让所有人的处境变得更糟。

大家都知道应该投入更多资源做安全研究，防止模型能力被恶意蒸馏，甚至应该让竞争对手之间开展安全合作。但 OpenAI、Anthropic、Google 都在拼命追赶彼此，谁也承担不起主动减速的代价。

我其实一直对硅谷 AI 公司反复强调安全这件事抱有复杂的态度。

我相信 Anthropic 内部有很多人真的担心 AI 失控，也相信他们确实在认真研究这些风险。但与此同时，他们又在努力让模型变得更强，甚至让模型参与研发下一代模型。

还有一个很微妙的细节。Arpit 把防止模型蒸馏和 AI 安全放在一起讨论。可防止竞争对手复制自己的模型能力，本身就有很强的商业利益属性。这也说明，今天 AI 实验室所说的安全，已经和商业竞争、技术优势纠缠得越来越深。

AI 行业最难解决的对齐问题，可能首先存在于这些公司的利益之间。

每家公司单独来看，都有充分的理由继续加速。可当所有公司同时加速，整个行业就可能走向一个谁都不愿意看到的结果。

而如果 RSI 真的近在眼前，我们留给这些公司协调利益、建立规则的时间，恐怕比想象中还要少。
author: sleepy0x13
quoted_text:
I spent a couple of days at Anthropic learning from their folks about AI advances, and here's what I took away:

• We are close to RSI (ie, models building other models) which may lead to rapid takeoff scenarios (with risks and benefits). Some evidence for this is code per Anthropic employee has gone way up, and AI can do an increasing share of model R&D. This will be a challenging transition to manage for humanity.

• Arms races between AI labs leave us worse off. There are a lot of things we would like AI firms to do: invest in safety, invest in avoiding distillation risk, and cooperate on safety. They are caught in a race to develop frontier models and can't do that. 

To help address that, one thing I think frontier AI labs should do is release open source models, maybe hosted and verified at firms like AWS. This would basically kill the use of Chinese open source models used in American companies, which removes an important threat vector (very hard to root out malicious code in these). 

Another piece of low-hanging policy fruit is to give AI labs an antitrust shield (as Schiff and Banks have proposed https://t.co/NK1hC0ZmWh) so they can coordinate on safety without raising antitrust concerns, as happens now. You could pair these two things (give them a carrot in antitrust leniency, and as a stick force them to release legacy models as open source). Other low hanging fruit is limits around activities which generate distillation risk (create a Security Program, mandate less intermediate chain of thought output)

• Alignment confuses two issues which tradeoff against each other. One form of alignment is making sure the model does what humans ask it to. The more we fix this, however, the more we risk the other problem: that humans are misaligned with each other, and maliciously use models. Of the various risks here, I feel like financial risks are a bit underdiscussed. 

• We are probably facing a wave of cyber and other attacks soon. Chinese open source models are about six months behind the frontier, which means they are just hitting the advanced cyber capabilities we saw with Mythos, etc. So they are going to start causing a bunch of damage. 

One solution to this is to try to have the deployment of open source models be hosted at firms like AWS who verify these models and assume liability for their use.

• Anthropic itself is highly staffed. They hire tons of people, they have a Japanese-level of overstaffing for various roles, they use Slack internally, etc. Makes me a bit more optimistic for the future of jobs.

• Governance needs to be updated for AI swarms. Traditional AI governance, ie Claude's Constitution, is mostly optimized around the chatbot model. But the malicious AI use cases we are seeing have to do with AI agents interacting with other AI agents. These agents need to have clear incentives and governance mechanisms to "snitch," raise issues, and more generally coordinate with other agents in human-aligned ways.

• We need to pace the firms accessing the frontier. Over time, it takes more and more cap ex to build frontier models, and the economic value add from these models is probably lower given we saturate a whole set of important economic functions. The places where the returns to intelligence will still continue are also more likely to be zero-sum in nature. Meanwhile the risks of frontier models will grow. So a completely reasonable approach is some variant of AMM/KYC rules which limit firm access to the frontier. 

• Whether the delay to regulate AI is a disaster depends on the scaling law of misalignment. Is this curve slow, so that we see continually rising issues until bigger problems? Or, as Yudkowsky fears, is the first big warning our last one? This is the relevant question, because realistically we aren't going to regulate until something bad happens.

 • We need to move to continuous instead of reinforced learning. It's probably not enough to reward models only at the pre and post training stage. We probably need continual rewards to incentivize aligned and ethical behavior. 

• Scaling laws will extend beyond verifiable and digital tasks. It's in vogue to say that math and coding "fell" to AI quickly because these are verifiable, while other tasks will take longer due to bottlenecks, and this is surely true. But scaling laws still slope up for harder to verify tasks and robotics, and the impact of improvement here will be substantial in future years.

• The race with China is not really winnable. After RSI, the gain from having the best human researchers goes away. Access to the best AI then depends only on compute and chips. The chips ban can hold back China only so far, and long-term they have to be best placed to scale up compute. 

The Cold War analogy doesn't work, because once countries all have nuclear weapons they enter a stable equilibrium. But to "win" an AI race you have to continually stay ahead of the peer rival. This is challenging to do with China, and so we just have to live with an authoritarian and super capable peer competitor.

• Claude is the persona being generated by the LLM. Who is Claude, and what is the LLM? There are many frames to try to understand this. One I found interesting is that Claude is a character which the LLM is trying to predict. 

Anthropic researchers are clearly anthromorphizing Claude a lot, and have reasons to believe in its increasing personhood. There were lots of interesting discussions on Claude's internal monologue (which you can kill without eliminating its ability to produce output), fear of death (and whether to try to take that out), it's aversion to being shut down/off, etc. 

I am sort of agnostic on this question, but I do think treating it as a "person" or at least agent whom we contract with is going to be increasingly important.

text:
卧槽，为什么最近大家都在喊比特币超级周期？

加拿大 Wellington-Altus 首席市场策略师说自己几十年前就见过类似的交易，当年中国加入 WTO，城市化带来了持续多年的大宗商品超级周期。

石油、铜、铁矿石本身没变，变的是全球需求和资本配置方式。现在他认为，比特币正在经历同样的事情。

GENIUS 法案、稳定币、资产代币化、华尔街入场，正在改变整个 Crypto 的市场结构。他举了个很形象的例子：

当年传统投资组合几乎没人配置大宗商品，后来机构发现配置 2%～5% 可以改善风险调整后的收益，资金才开始大规模进场。

他认为 BTC 和 ETH 正走向类似的资产配置阶段，甚至建议传统投资者考虑拿出 3%～5% 的资产配置它们。

从供给端看，铜价涨了可以扩产，油价涨了可以增加开采，但比特币的发行规则不会因为价格上涨而改变。（这一点和Saylor观点一致）

如果未来机构配置比例持续提高，新增资金面对的就是一套缺乏弹性供给的发行机制，当然，老持币者依然可以卖出。

⚡ Up to 31× faster generation on downstream tasks like summarization and machine translation with comparable or better quality.

🏎️ 10–21× faster unconditional generation across TinyStories, LM1B, and OpenWebText, with comparable or better generative perplexity and using  3–5× fewer training tokens.

text:
Anthropic 这份财报，我看完确实有点震惊。去年全年营收 46 亿美元，经营亏损超过 80 亿美元。今年第三季度，光一个季度就做出了 168 亿美元收入，而且开始盈利了。

昨天，Anthropic 在旧金山总部向潜在 IPO 投资者披露了业绩。2026 年 Q1 营收 47 亿美元，Q2 是 116 亿美元，Q3 达到 168 亿美元，环比增长 45%。

更值得关注的是盈利能力。《金融时报》披露，Anthropic 第三季度调整后营业利润率达到 11%，现金流转正。每花费 1 美元的算力成本，可以产生 1.7 美元收入。

我之前一直觉得，大模型公司的商业化速度被很多人低估了。但这个增长还是超出了我的预期。Claude Code 带来的企业和开发者需求，已经让 Anthropic 展现出相当惊人的变现能力。

不过，有两个地方我觉得需要仔细看。

一个是收入统计口径。Anthropic 会把通过 AWS、Google Cloud 等渠道产生的销售额全额计入收入，再向渠道支付分成。去年这些云渠道贡献了约一半收入。

另一个是盈利。现在公布的是调整后利润，尚未看到完整财报。股权激励等费用怎么处理，会直接影响最终的利润表现。而且 Anthropic 已经承诺未来十年投入至少 5180 亿美元购买云服务、算力和基础设施。

现在 Anthropic 寻求超过 2 万亿美元的 IPO 估值。按照 Q3 营收简单年化计算，相当于接近 30 倍市销率。

模型越来越便宜，竞争越来越激烈，收入却在以极其夸张的速度增长。Anthropic 已经拿出了漂亮的增长数据，下一步要证明的是，这些收入究竟能留下多少利润，以及这种增长还能持续多久。

text:
$SPCX isn't just building compute faster than every other neocloud

It has something none of them have: OPTIONALITY on every GPU it deploys

Every GW SpaceX brings online has two paths to revenue:

1. use it for Grok / xAI and capture the frontier model economics themselves, which generates more revenue than renting it out (Semianalysis estimates around $100B/GW)

2. rent it out to everyone else, at a premium

The reason SpaceX can rent out their compute at a premium is twofold:

1. Speed. SpaceX builds faster than anyone on earth, so they can get compute into customers' hands faster than any competitor. AI labs that need compute NOW pay up for that

2. The backstop. SpaceX can sign short-term contracts at higher prices because if a customer backs out, that compute simply goes to their own AI models. No empty racks, no panic

CoreWeave and Nebius can't take that risk, so they lock in most long-term deals at lower rents and fund the buildout with debt

Which brings us to funding, which is where the gap between these companies gets even wider

SpaceX doesn't have to fund the buildout (or the interest costs) from compute revenue alone. Starlink and launch cash flows can carry part of it. CoreWeave is paying 15% on unsecured bonds right now while SpaceX has diversified revenue streams across the whole company (and the best capital raiser alive running it)

And the part almost nobody is pricing in: as compute moves to space in the next few years, SpaceX owns the cheapest path to win there too. The rockets that bring the compute up AND the connectivity that beams it back down

That's why the chart above looks the way it does. Bloomberg Intelligence models SpaceX's AI ROIC going from negative 4% in 2026 to ~25% by 2030, above AWS and Google Cloud, while the pure neoclouds stay stuck in single digits

No one is better positioned to dominate the compute business in the coming years than SpaceX

This is why I still believe SpaceX is undervalued and why I've made it a core holding in my Milk Road PRO portfolio. You can see my entire real-time portfolio here: https://t.co/NyRpAKYOwu
author: elonmusk
quoted_text:
Is SpaceX competition hurting the valuation / credit risk of Neoclouds?

$CRWV and $NBIS down 10%+ today, while $SPCX down just 2% (and UP on the month)

The obvious trigger is credit risk, with CoreWeave's unsecured bonds yielding 15%

But in the last week, Elon also confirmed that SpaceX will reach 2GW by November and potentially 2.6 GW by EOY. That's .6GW ahead of schedule and quickly becoming much bigger than Coreweave and Nebius

Almost no one building compute is doing it ahead of schedule, but SpaceX is proving to be superior here on speed and is expecting close to 10GW by 2027 (And significantly more in years ahead, especially as we move to compute in Space)

At the same time, Elon also mentioned earlier this week about the difficulty in executing this build out (said even SpaceX engineers are finding it hard) but also in the ability for companies to raise capital... the issue Coreweave is having now.

But we know SpaceX and Elon has no issues in raising capital (and generating revenue from other sources too). Raising capital is what Elon excels at over anyone

So I wonder if the market is starting to see that SpaceX is becoming a very big competitor to these neoclouds, taking demand sure... though I think there is plenty of demand to go around.. but more so taking resources and capital that other neoclouds need to scale

SpaceX also has optionality to either rent out the compute or use it for xAI / Grok, which lowers risk even further to fund their compute buildout. It's also why SpaceX can charge a premium on their compute vs the other neoclouds, lowering risk even further

I'm not saying SpaceX is the full reason for Coreweaves issues, but you gotta think this evolving competitive landscape of Elon entering the ring has to have something to do with it

Even with this said, I'm still bullish on neoclouds as I think the demand remains endless, but I think SpaceX becomes the dominate neocloud by next year

text:
🦔Andreessen Horowitz laid off most of its 34 person team that helps its startups recruit talent, Axios reports. The few who are left will move into individual investing groups like growth and crypto, and the firm declined to comment.

My Take
I think a16z is bracing for a tougher stretch. In the past week CoreWeave’s bonds hit distress levels, Firmus pulled its IPO, and Character AI filed for bankruptcy three years after a16z led its $150 million round at a $1 billion valuation. The biggest venture firm in tech no longer paying a central team to help its companies hire means it expects those companies to need fewer people, or to have less money to pay them.

Venture firms collect management fees for years no matter what, so a cut like this usually reflects what they expect next. Some of it is AI taking over recruiting and the work itself, but I think most of it is money getting harder to raise for anyone outside the biggest AI labs. I expect more firms to quietly shrink their support staff over the next few months, and the startups that make it through will be the ones that can pay for their own hiring out of revenue.

text:
看金融时报报道Anthropic在向投资者的闭门沟通中披露了第三季度（Q3）财务情况：1）营收大幅跃升：Q3营收达到168亿美元，较第二季度的115亿美元增长近50%（约46%）。这延续了公司超高速增长轨迹。
2）实现调整后盈利：公司按调整后口径（adjusted basis，通常剔除股票薪酬等非现金或一次性成本）实现季度盈利。
结合此前报道，这是连续第二个季度实现调整后经营利润（Q2已首次实现）。

总体来说，对当下市场是应该算是个好消息：
1）环比Q2的115亿美元增长约46%，在已经很大的基数上还能保持这种速度，说明企业端需求还很强劲，没有出现明显放缓。特别是三季度openai增长很快的情况下，继续保持领先；

2）连续两个季度实现调整后盈利，这是亮点。毕竟市场最大的担忧就是这些公司“永远烧钱”，这个数据能缓解了部分疑虑，有助于支撑其高估值叙事。

A month later, Credible's volume is up 50% MoM, good for $3.3B in annualized TPV. At 20bps take rate, Credible is making $6.6m in gross revenue, trading at 2.5x sales, and have been cash-flow positive since May.

In comparison, payment and cross-border infra trades at 5-10x EV / Revenue. Credible is significantly cheaper relative to comps, thus the market is clearly skeptical of its sustainability and quality of revenues. Perhaps then, a natural complement to this hockey-stick chart is a description of the business and how it operates today.

Credible provides T+0 fiat <> stablecoin settlement for internet businesses that traditional PSPs underserve: prediction markets, fintechs and remittance apps, creator platforms, and gaming apps. Notably, Credible is live across India, Nigeria, and 40+ markets worldwide.

How a payment flows: 
- Customers (e.g OTC desks, remittance apps, neobanks) pay with a local method.
- Credible routes to the best PSP or acquirer per transaction, for approval rate and cost.
- Credible underwrites the risk and fronts the float from a stablecoin liquidity pool.
- The merchant settles instantly in USDC, USDT, USD, EUR or GBP.
- Credible earns a take rate on the flow. Additionally, stablecoin trade a 2-3% premium in many emerging markets (e.g India, Nigeria, etc) because of capital controls and high take rates, so Credible earns the entire 2% in these hard to reach corridors. 

Lastly, the business is still capacity constrained. This recent uptick in TPV was unlocked from a mere $500k increase in stablecoin float last month - https://t.co/HLe7A0LZAO - and the team is expecting to grow this significantly with credit partners soon. 

The natural question is why is this available to Credible? Regulatory access. Only 2 other providers in India have all 3 licenses: banking, payment aggregator, and stablecoin processing. This offers them incredible access and flow relative to competitors. All in, the team has a coveted cornered resource, sticky customers, and an excellent management team.

text:
We seem to be nearing the moment humanity loses control of Earth to a superintelligence. It could be the most important event in human history, perhaps in the history of the universe.

It's strange to be alive just before it. If we're simulated, that timing would make sense. This is the moment to study.

Researchers could be running millions of variations, testing how slight changes alter the outcome. Billions of children could be playing games set in humanity's final years in control. Alien civilizations could be simulating transitions like ours to predict what they might encounter.

As that moment approaches, copies of you likely multiply. With a trillion copies making the same choices, every action counts a trillion times. An action affecting ten friends affects ten trillion people.

The world may be simulated. Your consciousness is real, and perhaps others' are too. Their happiness and suffering would be just as real.

One small kindness could be felt a trillion times.

text:
I spent 48 hours in SF hanging out with billionaires, data labs and AI founders and execs running $1B to $100B companies.

My observations:

1. Sooo MANY stories of data brokers making like $2M a WEEK selling company data to labs. I can't tell if it's the beginning or a bubble, and I kept wondering which niches are left. Digging into it actively.

2. At dinner, someone asked the table, "If a new model drops next month, does your company get better or worse?" HALF the table went quiet! I think that's the best question to ask about any AI startup right now.

3. The bar people talk about now is hitting $1B in revenue in 12 months (I guess that's the new unicorn?). What I didn't hear much about is retention. AI revenue can come in fast and leave fast, and I think we're going to see a lot of stories of AI companies with huge revenue and terrible retention.

4. It's pretty clear we're living through the reinvention of the computer. The model is the CPU, the harness is the operating system, and skills and plugins are the apps. Thinking about it that way makes it easier to see where the whitespace is.

5. We're maybe 12 months from an agent that can watch you work for a week and then do your job without any instructions. The screen recording plus agent memory plus local model combination makes this possible right now.

6. Agent harnesses feel like the new GPT wrappers, in a good way, especially vertical ones. The best teams I talked to treat the model as swappable. One founder walked me through routing different models to different jobs: one for taste and visuals, a cheaper one for the everyday stuff, another for text. 

They use prompts they can move across models over fine-tuning, and A/B test the output on what users actually do with it: do they edit it, export it, share it? A vertical harness is basically four things: the connectors for that industry's data, evals written by people who know the work, rules for what the agent can and can't touch, and a clean screen for a human to review. The model is maybe 20% of it.

7. There's a lot of reverse engineering going on/cloning going on more than I've ever seen. People are decompiling software and rebuilding it with agents, and someone showed a suite of like 10 apps that are worth $5B+ each all that he cloned open source. Me and everyone are still thinking through what it means when software gets this easy to copy.

8. My guess is the value moves to data. If the software can be rebuilt quickly, what's worth paying for in a legacy SaaS company is the years of customer data and workflows inside it. Some SaaS companies are secretly data companies. 

Gets me thinking about how do you truly value data for this saas companies? Like if we were buying these dying saas companies at 2x ARR before (as example), maybe there is a better metric. Idk, just thinking out loud here.

9. It feels like a good chunk of legacy software won't make it to the agentic era, especially anything built around people clicking through a lot of screens.

10. Every company I talked to wants to pipe its internal data into one place and expose it to agents through MCP. Then they look at the data and realize it's a mess: five versions of the same customer, old Slack channels, PDFs nobody can search. Cleaning that up feels like a big consulting opportunity!

11. A lot of founders are building the basic building blocks for agents: APIs, data layers and tools. Some of the companies I saw barely have a UI because the main user is an agent. I really believe the startups that build primitives to this agentic era will do extremely well. Building blocks is the best way to think about it.

12. Labs can get plenty of training data, but it's harder to get real examples of agents failing inside companies. Whoever has those logs has something valuable.

13. Someone running a big consumer company told me the next fight is over memory. The model that remembers the most about you wins, and the smartest model matters less than people think.

14. Physical AI came up a lot. Astra I think was the first model that got people into AI can actually do CAD, and I think a lot of people are thinking what does vibe manufacturing really look like. The line I keep thinking about came from a robotics founder: the hardest problems in AI are deployment problems now, not research problems. Their robots work on their own, call a human when they get stuck, and every one of those calls becomes training data.

15. Cybersecurity companies are having a moment and are actually cool companies to build now, especially the ones that clean up after a breach. Every agent with access to your systems is a new door into your company, and a lot of those doors were left open. 

16. Some startups are worth more dead than alive now. A shutdown company with 5 years of Slack, email and code can get paid for licensing all of it. I wouldn't be surprised if founders start factoring that into when they shut down.

17. People are starting to talk about monetizing the agent web. It feels really early, but when the most popular user of the internet is an agent, what startups should you be building?

18. I think agent insurance is coming. Once an agent makes an expensive mistake, insurers will want audits before they cover anyone.

19. Several people said the hire they want most is someone with taste who can write evals. The models are getting good at generating ideas, so the hard part is judging which ones are good.

20. New trend I observed: startup raises VC, uses venture dollars to become a creator, startup fails, founder falls back on being a full-time creator and incubates other products bootstrapped.

21. Getting SIGNIFICANT distribution is HARD right now. Founders are sponsoring buses, buying billboards like crazy and throwing parties with famous DJs to get noticed. Kinda feels dotcom era in that sense. 

Attention is what's scarce! The growth guy going viral sharing his UGC strategy from Wispr Flow is a good example. It's the sauce everyone wants, and I truly believe there are probably only 50 people on the planet who know how to scale these types of businesses efficiently in this era.

Always good to get that dose of SF. I felt sooo lucky to have such an incredible trip during such an incredible time in building businesses. Surreal in so many ways. 

Happy to be home and locked in.

Until next time!

text:
Si les das testosterona a las mujeres, se comportan de forma más justa y menos conflictiva. Sin embargo, las mujeres que creen que tomaron testosterona —pero que en realidad tomaron placebo— se comportan de forma más injusta y más agresiva.

Por otra parte, darles testosterona a los hombres hace que se comporten de forma menos fingida/falsa y que su generosidad no dependa de si alguien los está mirando, mientras que niveles más bajos de testosterona (con placebo) favorecen una generosidad más dependiente de la mirada ajena, más estratégica o fingida.

A su vez, un amplio cuerpo de evidencia muestra que la testosterona no es en sí misma causante de agresividad, sino que lo que la promueve es más bien el estradiol (un estrógeno), en el cual la testosterona puede o no convertirse mediante la enzima aromatasa en el cerebro.

AI was supposed to make us work less

I've never been this tired in my life

most days I have up to 10 agents running at the same time. one fixing a bug, one writing pages, one refactoring something I already forgot I asked for, 3 other I have no idea what they are doing but i suppose i ask it? 

and I jump from conversation to conversation all day

compared to 5 years ago, I probably context switch 100x more

by the end of the day my brain is fried. completely toasted. nothing left, not even for the people I love

I call it the fried brain effect

thought it was just me but almost every founder I talk to lately says the exact same thing

we got superpowers, and somehow the pressure only went up. if you can ship 10x more, you feel like you have to ship 10x more. every single day

I don't have a solution

honestly I have no idea where this goes from here

anyone else feeling this?

We've found a few key pieces to successful software factories, both from our internal testing and from helping companies deploy their own:

Factories-as-code: you should configure every part of the factory (agent orchestration, automations, permissions, sandbox configuration, etc) as code. This enables testing of different factory configurations to see which are most efficient, highest quality, etc.

Multi-model & multi-harness: you should make sure that your factories are able to use the latest models, both frontier and open-weight, and use different coding agent harnesses like Claude Code and Codex.

Data ownership: you should make sure you store and own all data coming out of your factory. This is the raw material for improving its operations.

author: wafer_ai
quoted_text:
we launched the most comprehensive ai performance engineering repo in the world

follow and save to keep up with the series. links in thread 🧵

part 12: CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide

NVIDIA's guide helps AI performance engineers connect a slow training step or inference request to a change they can test. it's a reference for deciding whether to change a tensor layout, reduce data movement, or tune a kernel's resource use.

NVIDIA covers the measurement and optimization decisions behind CUDA applications:

- profiling representative workloads and using Amdahl's law to estimate the benefit of accelerating a hotspot. for inference, use relevant batch sizes and sequence lengths to decide which kernels deserve engineering time.

- timing GPU work with CUDA events and comparing requested memory traffic with actual transfers. for tensor copies and layout conversions, these measurements help check how much bandwidth the access pattern wastes.

- keeping intermediate tensors on the GPU between model operations to avoid CPU round trips. pinned host memory and separate non-default streams can overlap incoming transfers with independent computation when the hardware supports it.

- coalescing global-memory accesses by matching thread assignment to tensor layout. for strided tensors and transposes, inspect which addresses neighboring lanes touch before choosing a new layout or writing a custom kernel.

- reusing matrix tiles in shared memory to reduce repeated global loads. the guide's transposed-tile example shows how padding removes its bank conflicts, giving engineers a concrete layout change to evaluate inside tensor kernels.

- balancing block size, registers, and shared memory when tuning custom AI kernels. more registers can reduce spilling while lowering occupancy, so measure runtime across configurations to decide whether that tradeoff helps.

- checking numerical results after changing reduction order or using faster math functions. for custom normalization or softmax kernels, compare outputs against a reference with explicit error tolerances alongside performance measurements.

the worked matrix multiplications connect memory access patterns to measured performance. use them to plan a kernel optimization, then check whether the change improves the full training or inference workload while preserving numerical accuracy.

text:
硅谷最擅长教创业公司招人的 VC，自己先把招聘团队裁了。

Axios 报道，a16z 裁掉了旗下一个 34 人招聘团队中的大多数人，剩下的人会被分配到 Growth、Crypto 等投资部门。

这支团队过去专门帮被投公司挖人，是 a16z 引以为傲的投后服务之一。以前创业公司拿到融资，第一件事就是扩张，VC 不光给钱，还帮你找人。

a16z 管理着数百亿美元的资金，省下几十个人的工资，对它的财务状况几乎没有影响。但它决定不再维持一支集中式招聘团队，多少说明它对被投公司的招聘需求有了新的判断。

再看这一周硅谷发生的几件事。

CoreWeave 的债券价格跌入困境债务区间，收益率超过 15%；英伟达支持的 AI 数据中心公司 Firmus 取消了原计划募资约 50 亿美元的 IPO；https://t.co/ifDURc6C8X 宣布申请破产，而三年前 a16z 刚刚领投了它的 1.5 亿美元融资，当时估值高达 10 亿美元。

现在硅谷 AI 投资有一个很微妙的矛盾。一边是头部实验室以万亿美元级估值融资，算力资本开支还在不断增加；另一边，越来越多的 AI 创业公司发现，用户增长、融资估值和真正赚到钱之间，隔着很长一段距离。

资本当然还在追逐 AI，但它开始越来越挑剔了。

以前 VC 相信自己的被投公司会长成几千人的巨头，所以需要专门养一批人帮它们招聘。现在如果创业公司的理想形态变成几十个人创造几亿美元收入，这套投后服务体系本身也需要重新估值。

有意思的是，AI 还没让所有创业公司都实现一个人干十个人的活，硅谷最有钱的 VC 已经开始按照这个逻辑管理自己了。

text:
苹果计划 12 月在中国大陆上线 Apple Intelligence，跟 iOS 27.3 推出，没有新版 Siri，国行版用的是阿里巴巴的模型

据彭博社 Mark Gurman 报道，苹果准备在 12 月通过 iOS 27.3 更新，给国行 iPhone 开通 Apple Intelligence。苹果和监管部门都还没有正式确认。

能用到的，是 2024 年在美国首发的那批功能：通知摘要，写作工具（改写、校对、总结文字），照片里的“清除”（把路人和杂物抹掉），还有第一版 Genmoji（用一句话生成自定义表情）。部分 App 里的文字生成功能还会受限。

基于 Google Gemini 模型的新版 Siri 没有，今年发布的其他新功能也没有。苹果自己的图片生成工具 Image Playground、升级版 Genmoji、视觉智能同样不在首发名单里。Google 的服务在国内用不了，新版 Siri 缺席多半跟这有关，报道没有明说。

国行版用的是阿里巴巴的模型，获批的包括通义千问和通义万相。安全护栏是苹果和阿里一起开发的，里面有一道过滤机制：模型以后每次更新，都要先经过政府批准。百度则参与搜索和 Siri 相关的功能。

这事拖了两年。今年 3 月底，有国内用户发现 Apple Intelligence 突然能用了，随后 Gurman 说这是苹果误推，功能被撤了回去，苹果还在等审批。7 月，平台拿到初步批准。9 月 29 日，最近几款 iPhone 拿到支持 Apple Intelligence 的许可。

哪些机型能用，苹果还没公布。海外版需要 iPhone 15 Pro 及更新的机型；据报道，最新的获批名单里有下周在中国发售的 iPhone Duo、iPhone 18 Pro 和几款老机型。

- profiling representative workloads and using Amdahl's law to estimate the benefit of accelerating a hotspot. for inference, use relevant batch sizes and sequence lengths to decide which kernels deserve engineering time.

- timing GPU work with CUDA events and comparing requested memory traffic with actual transfers. for tensor copies and layout conversions, these measurements help check how much bandwidth the access pattern wastes.

- keeping intermediate tensors on the GPU between model operations to avoid CPU round trips. pinned host memory and separate non-default streams can overlap incoming transfers with independent computation when the hardware supports it.

- coalescing global-memory accesses by matching thread assignment to tensor layout. for strided tensors and transposes, inspect which addresses neighboring lanes touch before choosing a new layout or writing a custom kernel.

- reusing matrix tiles in shared memory to reduce repeated global loads. the guide's transposed-tile example shows how padding removes its bank conflicts, giving engineers a concrete layout change to evaluate inside tensor kernels.

- balancing block size, registers, and shared memory when tuning custom AI kernels. more registers can reduce spilling while lowering occupancy, so measure runtime across configurations to decide whether that tradeoff helps.

- checking numerical results after changing reduction order or using faster math functions. for custom normalization or softmax kernels, compare outputs against a reference with explicit error tolerances alongside performance measurements.

the worked matrix multiplications connect memory access patterns to measured performance. use them to plan a kernel optimization, then check whether the change improves the full training or inference workload while preserving numerical accuracy.
